checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one setting in your page design or SEO plugin, which names the same address on every page.

checks.title: Canonical points to a redirect
checks.description: The page's canonical names a URL that redirects. The detail gives the URL the redirects end at, or says that they lead back to this page. Where the crawl didn't check that URL, or was refused there, the detail says so: it is where the redirects lead, and may not be where they end.
checks.fix: Change the canonical to the redirect's final URL, which the detail gives; when the redirect leads back here, that's this page's own URL. If the detail says the URL wasn't checked, or was refused, open it first and use the address you end up at: it may redirect again.
checks.why: A canonical should name the final URL you want indexed. Naming a redirect sends search engines two signals that disagree: the canonical says to index the named URL, and its redirect says to index another. When the redirect leads back to this page, such as a canonical to /page on /page/ when /page redirects to /page/, this page most likely stays the indexed one, but the canonical is still wrong.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that name a forwarding address as their main one
plainWhat: These pages name a main address (a "canonical" link) that forwards visitors on to another address.
That gives search engines two answers to one question, and they may not pick the one you want.
Often it forwards straight back to the page itself, which does little harm but is still worth tidying.
plainFix: Look at where each main address in the list ends up: the list names the address, and says when it couldn't be checked.
Put that final address in the "canonical" box of your site's editor, often under "SEO", if it has one.
Ask your developer to correct it in the page design if the same thing shows on many pages.
checks.plainPassed: No page names a forwarding address as its main one
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one setting in your page design or SEO plugin, which names the same address on every page.

checks.title: Canonical points to a non-indexable page
checks.description: The page's canonical names another URL on the site that can't be indexed itself: it's noindex, canonicalised to yet another URL, or blocked by robots.txt. A URL that refused the crawler (a firewall, a bot challenge or a rate limit) isn't judged, as that says nothing about search engines; it's reported as blocked itself.
checks.fix: Point the canonical at the final, indexable URL. If the target isn't meant to be indexed, this page probably shouldn't name it as canonical.
checks.why: A canonical asks search engines to index the named URL instead of this one, so if that URL is noindex, blocked or points elsewhere in turn, the signals contradict each other and the outcome is up to Google. Google's own checklist includes making sure the canonical target isn't noindex. Canonical chains (A to B to C) usually come from content that moved more than once.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that name a main address search engines can't show
plainWhat: These pages name a main address (a "canonical" link) that can't itself appear in search results.
The page says "show that one instead", while that one says "don't show me", so the outcome is left to Google.
The list says what holds each one back, such as an instruction to stay out of search.
plainFix: Look at the main address the list shows for each page, and why it can't appear in search.
If that address should appear in search, ask your developer to remove what holds it back.
If it shouldn't, ask them to point the page's canonical link at its own address, or at one that can appear.
checks.plainPassed: No page names a main address that search can't show
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one setting in your page design or SEO plugin, which names the same address on every page.

checks.title: Canonical outside <head>
checks.description: The page's only canonical links are in the <body> as browsers parse it, and there's no canonical HTTP Link header.
checks.fix: Move the canonical into the <head>, as early as you can, and remove the element that ends the head early (or move it into the body).
checks.why:
Google only accepts rel="canonical" in the , so the page has no canonical in effect. Often the tag is in the head in the source, but an element that doesn't belong there, such as an , a
or stray text from a script or plugin, ends the head early and pushes everything after it into the body. The same break can push other head tags, such as hreflang, out too.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Main address written in the wrong part of the page
plainWhat: These pages name their main address (a "canonical" link) in a part of the page where search engines ignore it.
So the pages have no main address in effect, and Google chooses one itself.
It usually means something added near the top of the page's code, by a plugin or script, has pushed it out of place.
plainFix: Note any plugin, tracking code or banner added to the site lately, as one of them may be the cause.
Send the list to your developer: the canonical link must sit in the page's "head" section.
Ask them to move or remove whatever ends that section early.
checks.plainPassed: No main address is written in the wrong part of the page
checks.plainLooksFor: Main addresses written in the wrong part of the page

checks.title: Relative canonical URL
checks.description: The canonical in the HTML is a relative URL, such as /page or //example.com/page, instead of a full URL with https:// and the host.
checks.fix: In the canonical link, write the address as a full URL, with the scheme and host, not a path on its own.
checks.why: Google supports relative canonicals, but recommends absolute URLs because relative ones can cause problems later, for example when a testing copy of the site gets crawled and its canonicals point at itself. A mistyped relative path (page instead of /page) also resolves against the current folder. Low priority if the canonicals resolve to the right URLs.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Main address written as a partial address
plainWhat: These pages give their main address in a short form, such as /page, without "https://" and your site's name.
Google can read the short form, but recommends the full address.
A short form can end up pointing at the wrong place, for example on a test copy of the site.
If your main addresses already lead to the right pages, there's nothing to do now.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer when they next work on the site: it isn't urgent.
Ask them to write each page's main address (its "canonical" link) in full, starting with "https://" and your site's name.
checks.plainPassed: No main address is written as a partial address
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly how your page design or SEO plugin writes the main address on every page.
checks.plainLooksFor: Main addresses written as partial addresses

checks.title: Invalid canonical URL
checks.description: A canonical in the <head> or an HTTP Link header has a value that isn't a valid http or https URL, such as an empty href, an address with another scheme or a malformed one.
checks.fix: In the canonical link in the head, put this page's full URL, or remove the broken tag.
checks.why: Search engines can't resolve it, so it's ignored: if it's the page's only canonical, the page has none in effect. It's usually a template variable that didn't fill in.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages whose main address isn't a real web address
plainWhat: These pages name a main address (a "canonical" link) that is empty or isn't a real web address.
Search engines ignore it, which can leave the page with no main address at all.
It's usually a gap in the page design that was never filled in.
plainFix: Look at what the list shows for each page: it says whether the address is empty or badly formed.
Send the list to your developer and ask them to make each page name its own full address, or remove the broken line.
checks.plainPassed: No page names a main address that isn't a real address
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly a gap in your page design, which writes the same mistake on every page.

checks.title: Noindex page with a canonical to another URL
checks.description: The page is noindex and its canonical names a different URL, one that doesn't lead back to this page or to a broken URL.
checks.fix: If the page duplicates the other URL, remove the noindex and keep the canonical. If it should stay out of search, keep the noindex and make the canonical point to the page itself, or remove it.
checks.why: The two signals say different things: noindex asks for the page to be dropped from search, while the canonical says it's a duplicate whose signals belong to the other URL. Google hasn't documented which wins, and its guidance is to use rel="canonical", not noindex, to choose between duplicates on one site, since noindex removes the page from search entirely.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that give search engines two opposite instructions
plainWhat: These pages tell search engines to keep them out of search, and also name another page as their main version.
One instruction says "drop this page", the other says "treat it as a copy of that one", and Google doesn't say which wins.
Each page needs one or the other, not both.
plainFix: Decide, for each page, whether it's a copy of the page it names or a page that should simply stay out of search.
If it's a copy, ask your developer to remove the instruction to stay out of search (the "noindex").
If it should stay out of search, ask them to point its main address (its "canonical" link) at the page itself.
checks.plainPassed: No page gives search engines opposite instructions
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one setting in your page design or SEO plugin, which names the same address on every page.

checks.title: Paginated page canonicalised to page 1
checks.description: This later page of a paginated series, page 2 onward by its rel="prev" link or a page number in its URL (?page=2, ?p=2, /page/2/), names the series' first page as its canonical. It isn't reported as canonicalised too.
checks.fix: If the later pages' items are listed in the sitemap or linked from elsewhere, leaving the canonical on page 1 is a choice you can keep. Otherwise, on each later page of the series, point the canonical link at that page itself, and keep ordinary links between the pages.
checks.why: This is a common setup, often deliberate, and a setting in many SEO plugins and shop themes. The canonical asks search engines to treat each later page as a copy of page 1, so the pages of the series don't compete as duplicates. It matters when products or posts are listed only on later pages: they're then reached only through pages that ask to be treated as copies, so make sure they're in the sitemap or linked from elsewhere. Google's pagination guidance prefers each page of a series to name itself as its canonical.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Later pages of a list that point Google at the first page
plainWhat: These are page 2 onward of a list, such as a category, and each names the list's first page as its main version.
It's a common setup, often chosen on purpose.
Anything listed only on a later page is then reached only through pages that ask to be treated as copies.
Google's guidance prefers each page of a list to name itself.
plainFix: Leave it if it's deliberate and everything on the later pages is in your sitemap or linked from elsewhere.
Otherwise, ask your developer to make each page of the list name its own address as its main version (its "canonical" link).
Keep the ordinary links between the pages, such as "Next" and the page numbers.
checks.plainPassed: No later page of a list points Google at the first
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one setting in your shop or SEO plugin, which every list shares.

checks.title: Canonical points to another site
checks.description: The page's canonical names a URL on another host, outside the crawl, so the page asks to be treated as a copy of a page on another site. It isn't reported as canonicalised too. The detail names the host.
checks.fix: If this page is a copy of an article first published elsewhere, that's right: leave it. Otherwise point the canonical at this site's own URL for the page; a staging, old or development host in it usually comes from a template or a setting.
checks.why: Search engines may index the other site's page instead of this one and fold this page's signals into it, so it can disappear from search. That's correct for content republished from another site, and a disaster when a template or a migration leaves every canonical pointing at a staging host or the old domain.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that tell Google another website has the real copy
plainWhat: These pages name a page on another website as their main version.
Google may then show that website's page instead, and drop yours from its results.
That's right for an article first published elsewhere, but a mistake when it names an old domain or a test copy of your site.
plainFix: Look at the website each page names: the list shows it.
If it's your own old address or a test site, ask your developer to point each page's "canonical" link at its own address.
If the page really is a copy of another website's article, leave it.
checks.plainPassed: No page names another website as its main version

checks.title: Canonical loop
checks.description: Following this page's canonical, page to page and through any redirects, comes back to this page: two or more pages name each other as their canonical. The detail lists the loop. Its pages aren't reported as canonicalised to a non-indexable page too.
checks.fix: Choose the one page of the loop that should be indexed, give it a canonical to itself, and point the others' canonicals at it.
checks.why: Each page asks to be dropped for another that asks the same, so the canonicals cancel out and Google picks a page itself, which may not be the one you meant. It usually comes from two pages each set to the other by hand, or from one rule that rewrites canonicals undoing another.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that point Google at each other in a circle
plainWhat: These pages each name another as their main version, and following those leads back round to where it started.
The instructions cancel out, so Google picks one of the pages itself, which may not be the one you want.
plainFix: Choose which page of each circle should appear in search: the list shows the circle.
Ask your developer to make that page name itself as its main version, and the others name it (their "canonical" links).
checks.plainPassed: No pages point Google at each other in a circle

checks.title: Canonical header on a redirect
checks.description: This internal URL redirects, and its response also has a Link header naming, as canonical, a different URL from the one its redirects end at. The detail gives both.
checks.fix: Remove the Link header from the redirect, or make it name the redirect's final URL. It usually comes from a server or CDN rule that adds the header to every response.
checks.why: Search engines follow the redirect and ignore the rest of the response, so the header has no effect on search. It misleads only people and tools that read the headers, but it can show that a rule meant for pages is applied to every response.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: Forwarded addresses that also name a different main address
plainWhat: These addresses forward visitors to another page, and also name a different page as the main version.
Search engines follow the forwarding and ignore the rest, so this changes nothing in search.
It can only mislead people who check the address with a tool, so it isn't urgent.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer when they next work on the site.
Ask them to remove the "canonical" link the server sends with these addresses, or make it name where they lead.
checks.plainPassed: No forwarded address names a different main address

checks.title: Canonical contains a fragment (#)
checks.description: A canonical in the <head> or an HTTP Link header has a fragment, a part after # such as #reviews. The detail gives the fragment.
checks.fix: Remove the fragment, the part after the hash, from the canonical link's address, so it is the page's plain URL.
checks.why: Google says not to use a fragment in a canonical, as it generally doesn't support them: it drops the fragment, so the canonical usually works as meant all the same. The markup is still wrong, and a fragment can be a sign the canonical is built from the browser's address rather than set on purpose.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Main addresses with a # part that Google ignores
plainWhat: These pages give their main address with a # part at the end, such as #reviews.
Google ignores everything from the # on, so the main address usually still works.
It's still a mistake, and it can mean the address was copied from the browser rather than set on purpose.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer when they next work on the site: it isn't urgent.
Ask them to remove the # part from each page's main address (its "canonical" link).
checks.plainPassed: No main address has a # part
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly how your page design or SEO plugin writes the main address on every page.

checks.title: Canonical link with hreflang, lang, media or type
checks.description: A canonical <link> in the <head> also has an hreflang, lang, media or type attribute, so search engines don't use it as the page's canonical. The detail names the attributes. A crawl made before the crawler noted these attributes isn't checked.
checks.fix: Remove hreflang, lang, media and type from the canonical link. To point at another language or a mobile version, add a separate alternate link with hreflang or media.
checks.why: Those attributes describe an alternate version of a page, not the page's own preferred URL. Google says canonical annotations with hreflang, lang, media or type aren't used for canonicalization, so the page is left with no canonical from this link and Google chooses one itself. The usual cause is an alternate link written as rel="canonical" by mistake.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Main addresses written in a way Google ignores
plainWhat: These pages name their main address with extra details, such as a language or a screen size, that belong on other links.
Google then doesn't treat it as the page's main address at all, and picks one itself.
It's usually a link to a translated or mobile version, written as the main address by mistake.
plainFix: Ask your developer to remove the extra details ("hreflang", "lang", "media" or "type") from each page's "canonical" link.
If the link was meant to point at another version of the page, ask for it to be written as a separate link.
checks.plainPassed: No main address is written in a way Google ignores

checks.title: Canonical URL that no page links to
checks.description: Another page names this indexable page as its canonical, but no crawled page links to it, not even with a nofollow link or through a redirect, and no sitemap lists it (a sitemap page nothing links to is an orphan page). It's only checked when the crawl read every page that could link to it.
checks.fix: Link to this page wherever its duplicates are linked, such as menus and listings, or change those links to point here. If it shouldn't be the canonical, point the other pages' canonicals at one that is linked.
checks.why: A canonical tells search engines which URL to index, and links tell them it matters: a canonical page nothing links to sends mixed signals, and Google may choose a linked duplicate instead. Visitors browsing the site only ever reach the duplicates.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Main versions of pages that nothing links to
plainWhat: Other pages name these pages as their main version, but no page on your site links to them.
Visitors browsing your site only ever reach the other versions, and Google may choose one of those instead.
plainFix: Link to each of these pages wherever its other versions are linked, such as in menus and lists.
If a page shouldn't be the main version, ask your developer to point the others' "canonical" links at one that is linked.
checks.plainPassed: Every main version of a page has links to it

checks.title: Non-indexable URL in sitemap
checks.description: A sitemap lists this internal URL, but it can't be indexed as listed: it redirects, returns a 4xx or 5xx error, is blocked by robots.txt, is noindex or names another URL as canonical. URLs the crawler couldn't check aren't included: timeouts, firewall blocks, and URLs robots.txt refuses to this crawler but allows to Googlebot.
checks.fix: Remove the URL from the sitemap, or replace it with the final, indexable URL, such as the redirect target or the canonical. If the sitemap is generated, fix its filter rather than editing the file.
checks.why: A sitemap should list the URLs you want in search results, and Google treats every URL in it as a suggested canonical. Listing URLs that redirect, fail or ask not to be indexed contradicts your other signals and spends crawls on URLs that won't be indexed. It's usually a sitemap generator that doesn't filter by status, noindex or canonical.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: Sitemap addresses that can't appear in search
plainWhat: Your sitemap, the file that lists your pages for search engines, includes addresses that can't appear in search.
Each one forwards elsewhere, fails, or is kept out of search some other way: the list says which.
A sitemap should hold only the addresses you want found, and these waste search engines' visits.
plainFix: Look at the reason the list gives for each address.
If the address should be found, fix that reason: it's often listed as a problem of its own.
If it shouldn't, take it out of the sitemap, or list the address it forwards to instead.
Ask your developer to change how the sitemap is built if your site makes it for you and has no setting for this.
checks.plainPassed: No sitemap lists an address that can't appear in search

checks.title: Indexable page not in a sitemap
checks.description: This indexable page isn't in any sitemap the crawl read. It's only checked when the crawl finished and every declared sitemap could be read.
checks.fix: Add the page's full URL to your XML sitemap, as its own url entry, ideally by making the generator include every indexable page type.
checks.why: Search engines can still find it through links, and on a small, well-linked site that's enough: Google says sites of about 500 pages or fewer that are comprehensively linked may not need a sitemap. On large or fast-changing sites, a complete sitemap helps new and updated pages get discovered sooner. Leaving out some page types, such as filtered or paginated listings, can be deliberate. Login, account and basket pages don't belong in a sitemap: they're better kept out of search with noindex.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages missing from your sitemap
plainWhat: These pages can appear in search, but aren't in your sitemap: the file that lists your pages for search engines.
Search engines can still find them through links, which is enough on a small site.
On a big or fast-changing site, a full sitemap helps new pages get found sooner.
Leaving pages out on purpose is fine, and login, basket and account pages are better kept out of search altogether.
plainFix: Look down the list for pages you want found quickly, such as new products or articles.
Find the sitemap options in your site's SEO settings or plugin, and include the kinds of page that are missing.
Ask your developer to add them if your sitemap is built another way.
checks.plainPassed: No page is missing from the sitemap

checks.title: Sitemap can't be read
checks.description: A sitemap listed in robots.txt, a sitemap index or the crawl settings returned an error (including 404), didn't respond, or isn't valid sitemap XML. Reported on the home page; the detail lists up to three, with their errors.
checks.fix: Open the sitemap URL to see the error, then fix the file or the server: it must be valid XML, at most 50 MB uncompressed and 50,000 URLs. If the sitemap no longer exists, remove its reference from robots.txt or the sitemap index.
checks.why: Search engines get no URLs from a sitemap they can't fetch or parse: Google keeps retrying for a few days, then stops trying that URL. Well-linked pages are still found, but what the sitemap adds, such as quicker discovery of new and deep pages, is lost. A referenced sitemap that returns 404 is usually stale and only needs removing.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: A sitemap on your site can't be read
plainWhat: A sitemap your site points search engines to can't be read: it's missing, fails to load, or has mistakes in it.
A sitemap is a file that lists your pages for search engines, and they get nothing from one they can't read.
Pages with links to them are still found, but new pages may take longer to show up in search.
plainFix: Open the sitemap's address from the list in your browser, to see the error.
If your site's SEO settings or plugin make the sitemap, use them to build it again.
If the sitemap no longer exists, ask your developer to remove the line that names it from your rules file (its "robots.txt").
Send the error to your developer otherwise: the file must load and be a valid sitemap of at most 50,000 addresses.
checks.plainPassed: No sitemap fails to load or has mistakes in it
checks.plainLooksFor: A sitemap that can't be read

checks.title: No XML sitemap found
checks.description: The crawl found no sitemap: none is listed in robots.txt or the crawl settings, and there's none at /sitemap.xml. Reported on the home page, only when sitemap discovery was on and the crawl finished, and not when the site refused the crawler or /sitemap.xml gave no answer or a server error.
checks.fix: Publish an XML sitemap of your indexable pages (most CMSs can generate one) and add a Sitemap: line with its full URL to robots.txt.
checks.why: A sitemap isn't required: Google finds pages through links, and a small, well-linked site may not need one. It helps most on large sites, new sites with few links from elsewhere, and sites with pages that links don't reach. A sitemap at another path that's only submitted in Search Console isn't visible to this crawl, so this may not be a real gap.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: No sitemap found
plainWhat: The check found no sitemap: a file that lists your pages for search engines.
A small site whose pages all link to each other can manage without one, as Google finds pages by following links.
It helps most on big or new sites.
If you gave your sitemap straight to Google, in Search Console, it won't show here, and there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Look in your site's SEO settings or plugin: most can create a sitemap with one switch.
Ask your developer to add its address to the site's rules file for search engines (its "robots.txt"), so they all find it.
Check the site again: it can then also find pages missing from your sitemap, and pages in it that nothing links to.
checks.plainPassed: A sitemap was found, or the site names one

checks.title: Sitemap lists a URL on another host
checks.description: A sitemap lists this URL, but it's on a different host from the sitemap: another site, or another of this site's hosts, such as www in a sitemap on the bare domain; or on another scheme, such as an http:// URL in an https:// sitemap. The detail says how the URL answered, or which schemes differ.
checks.fix: List the URL as it is on the sitemap's own host now (usually where it redirects), or remove the entry. For a sitemap that deliberately covers several hosts, set up cross-submission through Search Console or robots.txt.
checks.why: The sitemaps protocol only accepts URLs on the sitemap's own host and drops the rest, so the page it was meant for isn't submitted. Google makes an exception for cross-submission: when every site involved is verified in Search Console and the sitemap is submitted there, or the other host's robots.txt references the sitemap. It's common after a move to or from www.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: Sitemap addresses outside its own website
plainWhat: Your sitemap lists addresses on another website, or on another version of your own, such as with or without "www".
Search engines drop those entries, so the pages they were meant for aren't put forward.
It's common after a site moves to or from "www".
plainFix: Compare the start of the addresses in the list with the start of your sitemap's own address.
Build the sitemap again from your site's SEO settings or plugin, so it lists each page at its current address.
Ask your developer to correct the web address your site is set to, if the sitemap keeps using the old one.
Take out any address that belongs to another website altogether.
checks.plainPassed: No sitemap lists an address outside its own website

checks.title: robots.txt doesn't name the sitemap
checks.description: The site's robots.txt has no Sitemap: line, though the crawl found a sitemap anyway: at /sitemap.xml, where crawlers look by convention, or in the crawl settings. Reported once, on the home page, when sitemaps were read and robots.txt answered. The detail names the robots.txt and where the sitemap was found.
checks.fix: Add a Sitemap line anywhere in robots.txt, with the sitemap's full URL. One line for each sitemap is fine.
checks.why: Search engines read robots.txt before anything else, and its Sitemap: line is how all of them learn where the sitemap is, not only the ones it was submitted to. A sitemap at /sitemap.xml is usually found without it; one anywhere else may not be.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: Your rules file doesn't say where your sitemap is
plainWhat: Your site's rules file for search engines (its "robots.txt") doesn't give your sitemap's address.
The check found the sitemap anyway, where search engines look first, so most will find it too.
Naming it in the rules file makes sure every search engine does, wherever the sitemap is.
plainFix: Look in your site's SEO settings or plugin for an option to add the sitemap to the "robots.txt" file.
Ask your developer to add a line to the "robots.txt" file that names your sitemap's full address, if there's no such option.
checks.plainPassed: Your rules file for search engines names your sitemap

checks.title: Sitemap over 50,000 URLs or 50 MB
checks.description: A sitemap lists more than 50,000 URLs, a sitemap index lists more than 50,000 sitemaps, or a sitemap file is bigger than 50 MB uncompressed: the limits Google and the sitemaps protocol set for one file. Reported once, on the home page; the detail lists up to three, with what each is over.
checks.fix: Split the file into sitemaps of at most 50,000 URLs and 50 MB each, and list them in a sitemap index; an index over 50,000 sitemaps needs splitting into several indexes. Most CMS sitemap plugins can be set to fewer URLs per file.
checks.why: Search engines don't read past a sitemap's limits, and Search Console reports such a file as an error, so the URLs past the limit, or all of the file's, may not reach them through the sitemap.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: A sitemap too big for Google to read
plainWhat: A sitemap on your site lists more than 50,000 addresses, or is bigger than 50 MB.
That's more than one sitemap file may hold, and search engines may not read the addresses past the limit.
Those pages then aren't put forward to search engines by the sitemap.
plainFix: Look in your site's SEO settings or plugin for the number of addresses in each sitemap, and lower it.
Ask your developer to split the sitemap into several smaller ones, listed in one sitemap of sitemaps, if there's no such setting.
checks.plainPassed: No sitemap is too big for search engines to read

checks.title: Sitemap near the 50,000-URL or 50 MB limit
checks.description: A sitemap lists 45,000 to 50,000 URLs, a sitemap index 45,000 to 50,000 sitemaps, or a file is between 45 and 50 MB uncompressed: within a tenth of what one file can hold. Reported once, on the home page; the detail lists up to three.
checks.fix: Split the file before it grows past the limit: several sitemaps, listed in a sitemap index. Most CMS sitemap plugins can be set to fewer URLs per file.
checks.why: Nothing is lost yet, but a site that keeps adding pages will pass the limit, and the URLs past it may then not reach search engines through the sitemap.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: A sitemap close to the size Google can read
plainWhat: A sitemap on your site lists between 45,000 and 50,000 addresses, or is nearly 50 MB.
That's close to what one sitemap file may hold, and nothing is lost yet.
As you add pages it will pass the limit, and search engines may then not read the addresses past it.
plainFix: Look in your site's SEO settings or plugin for the number of addresses in each sitemap, and lower it.
Ask your developer to split the sitemap into several smaller ones before it grows, if there's no such setting.
checks.plainPassed: No sitemap is close to the size search engines can read

checks.title: Empty sitemap
checks.description: A sitemap that loaded without an error lists no URLs and no sitemaps. Reported once, on the home page; the detail lists up to three.
checks.fix: Find out why it's empty: a sitemap plugin set to include nothing, a section with no pages yet, or a file left behind. If it isn't needed, remove it and its reference in robots.txt or the sitemap index.
checks.why: An empty sitemap does no harm by itself, but it usually means a sitemap that should list pages doesn't, or one left over that search engines keep fetching for nothing.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: A sitemap with nothing in it
plainWhat: A sitemap on your site loads without an error but lists no pages.
That does no harm by itself, but it usually means a sitemap that should list pages doesn't.
Or it's an old one left behind, which search engines keep fetching for nothing.
plainFix: Open the sitemap's address from the list in your browser, to see what's in it.
Check your site's SEO settings or plugin, in case that part of the sitemap is switched off.
If the sitemap isn't needed, ask your developer to remove it and the line that names it.
checks.plainPassed: No sitemap is empty

checks.title: URL listed in more than one sitemap
checks.description: More than one of the site's sitemap files lists this URL. The detail names the sitemaps that list it.
checks.fix: Keep each URL in one sitemap, usually the one for its kind of page. Repeats often come from two sitemap plugins at once, or a page listed under two sections.
checks.why: The sitemaps protocol allows it and search engines cope, so this is housekeeping: repeated entries make sitemaps bigger and harder to keep right, and can give one URL two different lastmod dates.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: Addresses listed in more than one sitemap
plainWhat: These pages are listed in more than one of your sitemaps.
Search engines cope with that, so this is tidying rather than a problem.
Repeats make sitemaps bigger, and the copies can disagree about when a page last changed.
plainFix: Look for two SEO plugins or settings that both make a sitemap, and switch one off.
Otherwise keep each page in the one sitemap for its kind of page.
checks.plainPassed: No page is listed in more than one sitemap

checks.title: Sitemap lastmod invalid or in the future
checks.description: Sitemap entries have a <lastmod> that isn't a date (sitemaps use W3C Datetime, such as 2026-11-17 or 2026-11-17T09:30:00+00:00) or a date more than a day after the crawl. Reported once, on the home page; the detail counts each kind, names the sitemaps, and gives the first wrong entry with what its lastmod says. A crawl made before the crawler read lastmod isn't checked.
checks.fix: In the sitemap, set each URL's lastmod to the real last change as a W3C date, such as 2026-11-17 or with a time, as most CMS sitemap plugins do when left alone. Don't set every entry to today's date, or any entry to a date in the future.
checks.why: Google uses lastmod only when it's consistently and verifiably accurate. Dates it can't read, or that haven't happened yet, show it they aren't, so it may ignore the sitemap's dates and find changed pages later.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: Sitemap dates that are wrong
plainWhat: Your sitemap gives some pages a last-changed date that isn't a date, or that hasn't happened yet.
Google uses these dates only when they're accurate, so it may ignore them all.
Pages you change may then show up changed in search later.
plainFix: Check your site's SEO settings or plugin: most fill in each page's real last-changed date when left to themselves.
Ask your developer to correct the dates, if your sitemap is made some other way.
checks.plainPassed: Every sitemap date is a real date in the past

checks.title: Missing title
checks.description: This indexable page has no <title> element, or its first one is empty.
checks.fix: Add one title element in the page's head, unique to the page and saying what it is. If a template fills it, the field for this page type is empty.
checks.why: Google uses the <title> as one of its main sources for the page's title link in search results, and browsers show it in tabs and bookmarks. Without one, Google builds the title link from headings, anchor text and other text on the page, which may not say what you'd choose. Google asks for every page to have one, so fix this first.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages with no title
plainWhat: These pages have no title: the text on the browser tab, and the link people click in search results.
Google has to make one up from other text on the page, which may not say what you'd choose.
Every page should have one, so fix these first.
plainFix: Open the page in your site's editor and fill in its title, often under "SEO" or "Search engine listing".
Write a title that says what the page is about, and add your site's name if there's room.
If a whole kind of page has no title, ask your developer to set it in the page design.
checks.plainPassed: Every page has a title

checks.title: Multiple titles
checks.description: This indexable page has more than one <title> element (titles inside SVG images don't count). The detail says how many.
checks.fix: Keep a single title element in the head, and turn off whatever adds the others: a second plugin, the theme, or a server rule.
checks.why: HTML allows only one per page, and browsers use the first. Which one search engines use isn't documented, so the title you wrote may not be the one considered. A second title usually means two systems, such as a theme and an SEO plugin, are both writing the page's metadata.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages with more than one title
plainWhat: These pages have more than one title in their code, where only one is allowed.
Browsers use the first, but search engines may use another, so the title you wrote may not be the one shown.
It usually means two parts of your site each write one, such as the page design and an SEO plugin.
plainFix: Check whether your site has two SEO plugins, or a page design with SEO settings of its own, both switched on.
Turn one of them off, so each page gets a single title.
If you can't find a second source, ask your developer what else adds a title to the page.
checks.plainPassed: No page has more than one title

checks.title: Title too long
checks.description: The page's title is wider than 580 pixels (the default, which can be changed in the analysis settings), about 60 characters of ordinary text, measured as Google's desktop results show titles: Arial at 20 px, with full-width characters such as Chinese, Japanese and Korean, and emoji, one em wide.
checks.fix: Shorten the title or move the important words to the front; cut repeated words and long brand suffixes.
checks.why: Google sets no length limit for titles, but truncates title links to fit the device width, so the end of a long title may not show. Width depends on the letters ("WWW" is more than four times as wide as "iii"), so pixels predict the cut better than characters: 580 px is about where Google's desktop results cut a title, after the last whole word that fits, and a rough guide, not a rule. Google may also rewrite titles that are long-winded or stuffed with keywords. With the important words first, a cut-off rarely matters.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Titles that may be cut off in search results
plainWhat: These pages have a title too long to show in full in search results, where there's room for about 60 characters.
That room is a width, so the number of characters is a rough guide.
Search results cut a long title off to fit the screen, so the last words may not show.
That's harmless when the important words come first, and then there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Open the page in your site's editor and find its title.
Move the words that matter most to the front.
Cut repeated words and long endings, such as a slogan after your site's name.
checks.plainPassed: No title is likely to be cut off in search results

checks.title: Title too short
checks.description: The page's title is narrower than 200 pixels (the default, which can be changed in the analysis settings), about 20 characters of ordinary text, measured as Google's desktop results show titles: Arial at 20 px, with full-width characters and emoji one em wide.
checks.fix: Describe the page in the title: add the specific topic, product or place and, if you like, the site name.
checks.why: Short isn't wrong: a brand or product name can be exactly right. But very short titles are often vague, such as "Home", "Products" or "Page 2", which Google's guidance warns against because they don't tell searchers what the page is or set it apart from similar pages.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Very short titles
plainWhat: These pages have a title narrower in search results than about 20 characters of ordinary text.
It's measured by width, as Google shows it, so the number of characters is a rough guide.
Titles like "Login" or "Products" don't tell a searcher what the page is, or whose.
A short title can be exactly right, such as a product name, and then there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Open the page in your site's editor and find its title.
Say what the page is about, and add your site's name if there's room.
Leave the titles that already say it all.
Skip pages nobody searches for, such as login and basket pages.
checks.plainPassed: No title is very short

checks.title: Duplicate title
checks.description: Another indexable page has the same title, ignoring case and spacing. The detail says how many other pages share it.
checks.fix: Give each page a title that says what's specific about it. If the pages really are the same, consolidate them with a redirect or canonical instead. When they're one page at two addresses, the same path with a query added (/login/ and /login/?register=true), don't write a new title: point the address with the query at the clean one with a canonical, or make it noindex.
checks.why: Google asks for distinct titles on every page, because identical ones make it impossible for searchers to tell pages apart, and it may rewrite title links that repeat boilerplate. Duplicate titles often mean duplicate pages, or a template that leaves out the distinguishing detail, such as the product, place or page number.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that share the same title
plainWhat: Two or more pages have the same title: the text on the browser tab, and the link people click in search results.
Searchers can't tell the pages apart, and Google may make up a title of its own.
It often means two addresses show the same page, or the site's design leaves out what's different, such as the page number.
plainFix: Open each page in your site's editor and give it a title that says what's specific to it.
If two addresses show the same page, keep one and ask your developer to forward the other to it.
If they differ only by what follows a "?", such as /login/ and /login/?register=true, they're one page, so don't write a new title.
Instead, ask your developer to point the longer address at the shorter one (a "canonical tag"), or to keep it out of search results.
checks.plainPassed: No two pages share a title

checks.title: Missing meta description
checks.description: This indexable page has no meta description, or its first one is empty.
checks.fix: In the page's head, add one meta description: a sentence or two specific to the page. On a large site, generate it from the page's own data, such as the product name, price and key features.
checks.why: Google writes most snippets from the page's content, but uses the meta description when it describes the page better, and says high-quality descriptions can improve the quality and quantity of search traffic. Without one, the snippet is whatever text Google picks. Descriptions don't affect ranking, so prioritise important pages, such as the home page and key landing pages.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages with no search description
plainWhat: These pages have no search description: the short text under a page's title in search results.
Without one (a "meta description"), Google picks some text from the page, which may not be what you'd choose.
It doesn't change where the page ranks, so start with the pages you most want people to click.
plainFix: Open the page in your site's editor and find the description box, often under "SEO" or "Search engine listing".
Write one or two sentences that say what the page offers.
Skip pages nobody searches for, such as login and basket pages.
checks.plainPassed: Every page has a search description

checks.title: Multiple meta descriptions
checks.description: This indexable page has more than one meta description. The detail says how many.
checks.fix: Keep a single meta description in the head, and turn off the other source, usually a second plugin or the theme writing one as well.
checks.why: HTML allows only one per page, and which one search engines use isn't documented, so you can't be sure the one you wrote is the one considered for the snippet. It usually comes from a theme and an SEO plugin both adding one.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages with more than one search description
plainWhat: These pages have more than one search description in their code, where only one is allowed.
Search engines may read either one (each is a "meta description"), so the text you wrote may not be the one used.
It usually means two parts of your site each add one, such as the page design and an SEO plugin.
plainFix: Check whether your site has two SEO plugins, or a page design with SEO settings of its own, both switched on.
Turn one of them off, so each page gets a single description.
If you can't find a second source, ask your developer what else adds a description to the page.
checks.plainPassed: No page has more than one search description

checks.title: Meta description too long
checks.description: The page's meta description is wider than 985 pixels (the default, which can be changed in the analysis settings), about 160 characters of ordinary text, measured as Google's desktop results show snippets: Arial at 14 px, with full-width characters and emoji one em wide.
checks.fix: In the page's meta description, put what matters in the first sentence and trim the rest, so it still works if a search result cuts it.
checks.why: There's no length limit, but Google truncates snippets to fit the device width, about two lines on a desktop, so the end of a long description may not show, and it often builds the snippet from page text anyway. Width depends on the letters, so pixels predict the cut better than characters; 985 px is Screaming Frog's default. With the key point first, the cut rarely matters.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Search descriptions that may be cut off
plainWhat: These pages have a search description, the text under their title in search results, too long to show in full.
Search results have room for about 160 characters, and cut off the end of a longer description (a "meta description").
That's harmless when the important words come first, so only pages where the cut loses the point need changing.
plainFix: Open the page in your site's editor and find its description, often under "SEO".
Put what matters in the first sentence.
Trim the rest to about 160 characters, or leave it if the opening already works.
checks.plainPassed: No search description is likely to be cut off

checks.title: Meta description too short
checks.description: The page's meta description is narrower than 400 pixels (the default, which can be changed in the analysis settings), about 65 characters of ordinary text, measured as Google's desktop results show snippets: Arial at 14 px, with full-width characters and emoji one em wide.
checks.fix: In the page's meta description, write a sentence or two that says what the page offers and who it's for.
checks.why: There's no minimum, but a very short description rarely summarises the page, and Google uses the meta description only when it describes the page better than the page's own text. A short one is fine if it says everything that matters.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Very short search descriptions
plainWhat: These pages have a search description, the text under their title in search results, shorter than about 65 characters.
One that short (a "meta description") rarely says enough, so Google often shows text from the page instead.
A short one that says everything that matters is fine, and then there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Open the page in your site's editor and find its description, often under "SEO".
Write one or two sentences that say what the page offers, and who it's for.
checks.plainPassed: No search description is very short

checks.title: Duplicate meta description
checks.description: Another indexable page has the same meta description, ignoring case and spacing. The detail says how many other pages share it.
checks.fix: In each page's meta description, write text that belongs to that page alone, or generate it from the page's own data.
checks.why: Google says identical descriptions aren't helpful when individual pages appear in search, and recommends a unique one per page, with site-level wording only on the home page and other aggregation pages. Repeated descriptions usually come from a template default.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that share the same search description
plainWhat: Two or more pages share one search description: the short text under a page's title in search results.
Searchers can't tell the pages apart, and Google tends to write its own text instead.
The shared text (a "meta description") often comes from a default that the site's design fills in.
plainFix: Open each page in your site's editor and find its description, often under "SEO" or "Search engine listing".
Write one or two sentences that say what's on that page and nowhere else.
Leave numbered pages of one list (page 2, page 3) until last: they matter least.
checks.plainPassed: No two pages share a search description
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly a default description that your page design or SEO plugin gives to pages without one of their own.

checks.title: Missing H1
checks.description: This indexable page has no H1 heading, or its H1s are empty (the alt text of an image inside an H1, such as a logo, counts as text).
checks.fix: Mark the page's visible main heading as a single H1 that says what the page is about. Text styled to look like a heading, but not marked as one, doesn't count.
checks.why: The H1 is the page's main heading, and screen reader users jump between headings to find their way, so a page without one is harder to scan. Google lists headings such as the H1 among its sources for title links, but says it can rarely rely on HTML semantics, so this matters mostly for readers. Often the visible main heading is just styled text.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages with no main heading
plainWhat: These pages have no main heading (an "H1"): the headline that says what the page is about.
People using a screen reader rely on headings to find their way, and the page is harder to scan.
Often the headline is there to look at, but isn't marked as a heading.
It matters more to readers than to search, so it can wait until you next edit the page.
plainFix: Open the page in your site's editor.
Select the headline at the top and set its style to "Heading 1".
If the headline is part of the page design, ask your developer to mark it as the H1.
checks.plainPassed: Every page has a main heading
checks.plainOneFix: If these pages share one page design, marking its headline as the main heading fixes them all.

checks.title: Multiple H1s
checks.description: This indexable page has more than one H1 element. The detail says how many.
checks.fix: Keep one H1 for the page's main heading. Change the others to H2 or lower, or to ordinary text if they aren't headings.
checks.why: Google says the number and order of headings don't matter for Search, so this isn't a search problem. For readers and screen reader users, one H1 naming the page with H2s for its sections gives the clearest outline, which is why MDN advises against multiple H1s. Often a logo or a sidebar title is marked up as an H1 by the theme.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages with more than one main heading
plainWhat: These pages have more than one main heading (an "H1"), where one headline for the page is clearest.
Google says this doesn't matter for search, so it's about readers: screen readers use the main heading to say what the page is.
Often the page design marks the logo or a side panel's title as a main heading too.
The gain is small, so it can wait.
plainFix: Open the page in your site's editor and see which lines are set to "Heading 1".
Keep that style for the page's headline, and set the others to "Heading 2" or plain text.
If the extra one is the logo or part of the page design, ask your developer to change it there.
checks.plainPassed: No page has more than one main heading

checks.title: Duplicate H1
checks.description: Another indexable page has the same H1, ignoring case and spacing. Pages in the same paginated series (joined by rel="next" and rel="prev") don't count against each other.
checks.fix: Make each H1 say what's specific about its page, such as the product, place or topic.
checks.why: Identical main headings make similar pages hard to tell apart for visitors arriving from search, and often signal duplicate pages or a template whose heading lacks the distinguishing detail. Google doesn't document duplicate headings as a problem in themselves, so it's low priority unless the pages are duplicates too.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that share the same main heading
plainWhat: Two or more pages have the same main heading (an "H1"): the headline that says what the page is about.
Visitors who land on one can't tell it from the other, and it often means the pages themselves are copies.
If the pages are clearly different in every other way, there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Open each page in your site's editor and look at its headline.
Change it to say what's specific to that page, such as the product, place or topic.
If two addresses show the same page, keep one and ask your developer to forward the other to it.
checks.plainPassed: No two pages share a main heading
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one heading in your page design, such as your site's name, marked as the main heading of every page.

checks.title: Heading levels skipped
checks.description: On this indexable page, which has an H1, a heading after the H1 is more than one level below the one before it (an H2, then an H4). Headings in menus and footers after the H1 count, as screen readers list them all; headings before the H1, such as a theme's hidden cart or a menu's column titles, aren't judged. The detail gives the first such step and quotes the heading it skips to.
checks.fix: Use the next heading level for each subsection: an H2 under the H1, an H3 under an H2. Style a heading with CSS instead of skipping a level to make it look smaller.
checks.why: Screen reader users move through a page by its headings, and a skipped level suggests a missing section. HTML asks for each heading to be at most one level below the one before. Search engines cope either way, so this is about structure and accessibility.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Headings that jump levels
plainWhat: These pages have headings that jump a level, such as a main section heading followed by a sub-sub-heading.
People who use screen readers move through a page by its headings, and a jump suggests a section is missing.
plainFix: Edit each page and use the next heading size down for each smaller section.
Change how a heading looks with your site's styles, not by picking a smaller heading.
checks.plainPassed: No page's headings jump a level

checks.title: H1 is an image
checks.description: This indexable page's first H1 has no text of its own: its text is an image's alt, as with a logo in the H1. The detail quotes the alt. A crawl made before the crawler noted this isn't checked.
checks.fix: Give the page a text H1 that says what this page is about. Keep the logo as an image outside that heading, or inside it beside the text.
checks.why: An H1 that's a logo says the same on every page, the site's name, not what this page is about. Search engines read the alt, but a heading in text is clearer to them and to screen reader users.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Main headings that are pictures
plainWhat: These pages' main heading is a picture, such as your logo, with no words of its own.
It says the same on every page, your site's name, rather than what the page is about.
plainFix: Give each page a main heading in words that says what the page is about.
Keep the logo as a picture beside it, or elsewhere on the page.
checks.plainPassed: Every main heading is in words

checks.title: H1 or H2 over 70 characters
checks.description: This indexable page's first H1, or one of its H2s, is longer than 70 characters (the default, which can be changed in the analysis settings). The detail gives the first: its level, its length and its text.
checks.fix: Shorten the heading to what the section is about, and move the rest into the text below it.
checks.why: A heading is read as a label: a long one is harder to scan, and on a phone it wraps over several lines. Search engines read it whole, so this is about readers, not ranking.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Headings that run on
plainWhat: These pages have a main heading or section heading longer than 70 characters.
A long heading is harder to take in at a glance, and on a phone it wraps over several lines.
plainFix: Shorten each heading to what the section is about, and move the rest into the text below it.
checks.plainPassed: No heading runs on

checks.title: Long page without an H2
checks.description: This indexable page has 500 or more words of its own (the default, which can be changed in the analysis settings) and no H2 to divide them. A short page doesn't need one, so it isn't asked of one.
checks.fix: Break the text into sections, each under an H2 that says what it covers.
checks.why: Subheadings let readers scan a long page and jump to what they need, and they help search engines see what each part is about.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Long pages with no subheadings
plainWhat: These long pages have no subheadings to break up their text.
Readers find it hard to scan a long page without them, and to find the part they want.
plainFix: Divide each page's text into sections, each under a subheading that says what it covers.
checks.plainPassed: Every long page has subheadings

checks.title: Low word count
checks.description: This indexable page's main content has fewer than 200 words (the default, which can be changed in the analysis settings). Navigation menus and footers aren't counted.
checks.fix: Check whether the page is meant to be this short. If content is missing, restore it; if the page has little to offer, merge it into a related page with a redirect, or noindex it.
checks.why: Google says content length alone doesn't matter for ranking: there's no minimum word count. Plenty of good pages are short, such as contact, product and category pages. Use this to find pages that are empty by mistake, such as an unfilled template, a placeholder or content that only appears with JavaScript, not as a reason to pad pages out.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages with very little text
plainWhat: These pages have fewer than 200 words of their own, not counting menus and footers.
Short pages are often fine, and then there's nothing to do: a contact page doesn't need an essay.
This list is for spotting pages that are empty by mistake, such as one where the content failed to appear.
plainFix: Open each page and see whether anything is missing.
If content is missing, put it back.
If the page is meant to be short, leave it.
checks.plainPassed: No page has very little text

checks.title: Duplicate content
checks.description: Another indexable page has exactly the same main content: the same words in the same order, ignoring case and punctuation. Pages with fewer than 50 words (the default, which can be changed in the analysis settings) aren't compared.
checks.fix: Decide which URL should be indexed, then 301-redirect the others to it or give them a canonical pointing to it. If the pages should differ, give each its own content.
checks.why: Some duplication is normal and isn't against Google's spam policies. Google groups duplicates and shows one URL from the group, which may not be the one you'd choose, and crawls the others less often. The usual cause is the same page at several URLs, through parameters, trailing slashes or print versions.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages with identical content
plainWhat: Two or more pages have exactly the same main text, word for word.
Google shows only one of them, and it may not be the one you'd choose.
Usually it's one page that can be reached at several addresses, such as a print version or an address with extras on the end.
plainFix: Open the pages in each group and decide which address is the one you want found.
Ask your developer to forward the other addresses to it (a "301 redirect"), or to name it as their main address (a "canonical" link).
If the pages are meant to differ, give each one text of its own.
checks.plainPassed: No two pages have identical content

checks.title: Near-duplicate content
checks.description: Another indexable page has almost the same main content, roughly 96% or more alike (the default, which can be changed in the analysis settings). Exact copies are reported as duplicate content instead, and pages under that check's minimum word count aren't compared.
checks.fix: Give each page main content that is clearly its own, canonicalise the variants to one version, or merge them into one page with options.
checks.why: Pages that differ in only a few words, such as location pages with the town swapped or products that differ by size, may be grouped by Google as duplicates, with only one shown. That's fine for variants you don't need to rank separately. Pages that should rank on their own need differences that are, in Google's words, clear and significant.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages with almost identical content
plainWhat: Two or more pages have almost the same main text: only a few words differ.
Google may treat them as copies and show only one.
That's fine for versions you don't need found separately, such as one product in several sizes, and then there's nothing to do.
Pages that should each be found, such as one per town, need text that is clearly their own.
plainFix: Open the pages in each group side by side and decide whether each needs to be found on its own.
If so, give each page text that is clearly its own.
If not, ask your developer to name one of them as the main version (a "canonical" link), or merge them into one page.
checks.plainPassed: No two pages have almost identical content

checks.title: Duplicate version of the site
checks.description: This version of the site (the bare domain or www, over http or https) answers with a page, directly or after redirecting to another non-main version, instead of redirecting to the main version: the home page's.
checks.fix: 301-redirect every URL on the other versions to the same path on the main version, in one hop, at the server or CDN.
checks.why: Every page is then reachable at two or more addresses. Google treats the versions as duplicate URLs and picks one, preferring HTTPS, which may not be the version you want, and it crawls the copies less. If the duplicate is the http version, visitors who land on it browse unencrypted. The other version is only probed, not parsed, so a canonical on it isn't seen; a redirect is what makes the choice yours.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: Your site answers at more than one address
plainWhat: Your site shows its pages at more than one address, such as with and without "www", or on "http" as well as "https".
The spare addresses should forward to the main one.
As it is, search engines see two copies of everything and pick one themselves.
Visitors on an "http" copy also browse without encryption.
plainFix: Decide which address is the main one: usually the "https" one your home page uses.
Ask your developer or hosting company to forward every other version to it (a "301 redirect"), page for page.
Check the site again to confirm.
checks.plainPassed: The site answers at one address only
checks.plainLooksFor: A site that answers at more than one address

checks.title: Placeholder text (lorem ipsum)
checks.description: This indexable page's text, title or meta description has the placeholder "lorem ipsum" in it. The detail quotes it. A crawl made before the crawler looked for it isn't checked.
checks.fix: Replace the placeholder with the page's real text, or remove the block it's in, then check other pages made from the same template.
checks.why: Every visitor sees it, and it reads as an unfinished site. Search engines index it as the page's text, and it can end up in the snippet under the page's title.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages with dummy "lorem ipsum" text
plainWhat: These pages have the dummy text "lorem ipsum" on them, which designers use until the real words are written.
Every visitor sees it, and the site looks unfinished, and Google may show it under the page in search.
plainFix: Replace the dummy text with the page's real words, or remove the part it's in.
Check other pages made from the same design for it too.
checks.plainPassed: No page has dummy text

checks.title: Text that's very hard to read
checks.description: This indexable English page (its <html lang> is en or en-…) has a Flesch reading ease under 30 (the default, which can be changed in the analysis settings): long sentences of long words. Only prose is judged, 100 words and 5 sentences or more; menus and product grids without sentence ends aren't. A crawl made before the crawler counted sentences isn't checked.
checks.fix: Shorten long sentences, split ones that carry several ideas, and prefer short everyday words to long ones where they say the same.
checks.why: Text that's very hard to read loses readers before they reach the point, on phones above all. Flesch's scale puts under 30 at university level. Search engines don't score readability, so this is about the people reading.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Writing that's very hard to read
plainWhat: These pages' English text uses long sentences of long words, which makes it very hard to read.
Many readers give up before they reach the point, on phones above all.
plainFix: Shorten long sentences, split ones that say several things, and use everyday words where they mean the same.
checks.plainPassed: Every page's writing is readable

checks.title: Page mostly template text
checks.description: Under a quarter of this indexable page's words are its own: the rest are in its menus and footer. Pages with too few words of their own are another check's (low word count). The detail gives the page's own words of all its words. A crawl made before the crawler counted them isn't checked.
checks.fix: Add text of the page's own, or trim menus and footers that repeat long lists of links on every page.
checks.why: When most of a page is the same as every other page, search engines see little that's particular to it, and pages made from the template look alike to them.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that are mostly menus and footers
plainWhat: Less than a quarter of the words on these pages are their own: the rest are menus and footers.
Search engines see little on them that's different from your other pages.
plainFix: Add more of each page's own text about what it offers.
Trim menus and footers that repeat long lists of links on every page.
checks.plainPassed: Every page has enough words of its own

checks.title: Images without an alt attribute
checks.description: The page has elements with no alt attribute at all. Images with an empty alt="" (marked as decorative) and 1×1 tracking pixels don't count.
checks.fix: On each image that shows something, add an alt attribute that says what it shows or does on this page. On an image that is only decoration, add an empty alt attribute so screen readers skip it.
checks.why: Some screen readers read out the image's file name when there's no alt, and WCAG requires a text alternative for every image that conveys something. Google uses alt text, with computer vision and the page's content, to understand images for Google Images, and as the anchor text when an image is a link.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Images with no description
plainWhat: Some images on these pages have no description: the short text that says what an image shows.
People who can't see the image rely on it, and Google uses it to understand the image for image search.
An image that is only decoration needs no words, but should be marked as decoration so screen readers skip it.
plainFix: Open the page in your site's editor, select each image and fill in its description box, often called "Alt text".
Say what the image shows, in a few words, as you would to someone who can't see it.
Ask your developer to do the same for images in the page design, and to mark decoration as such (an empty "alt").
checks.plainPassed: No image is missing its description

checks.title: Alt text too long
checks.description: The page has images whose alt text is longer than 125 characters (the default, which can be changed in the analysis settings).
checks.fix: Cut the alt text to a short description of what the image conveys, and move longer descriptions, such as a chart's data, into a caption or the page text.
checks.why: W3C's guidance is that alt text should be the most concise description of the image's purpose, and anything longer than a short phrase or sentence belongs in a caption or the surrounding text. Screen reader users hear alt text in one go and can't skim it, and Google warns that alt text stuffed with keywords can make a site look spammy. 125 characters is a common convention, not a standard.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Image descriptions that are too long
plainWhat: Some images on these pages have a description, the text that says what an image shows, of more than 125 characters.
A screen reader reads the whole description aloud in one go, and its user can't skim it.
The limit is a rule of thumb, so a description just over it that reads well is fine to leave.
plainFix: Open the page in your site's editor, select the image and find its description box, often called "Alt text".
Cut it to a short phrase that says what the image shows.
Move longer detail, such as the figures in a chart, into a caption or the text beside the image.
checks.plainPassed: No image description is too long

checks.title: Images without width and height attributes
checks.description: The page has elements missing a width or height attribute, or both; 1×1 tracking pixels don't count. Only the HTML is read, so images sized in CSS still appear here.
checks.fix: On each image, set the width and height attributes to the file's real pixel size (CSS can still scale it), or give the image's box an aspect ratio or a fixed size in CSS.
checks.why: Without both attributes, and unless CSS gives the image box a size or aspect-ratio, the browser can't reserve space before the image loads, so the content below jumps when it arrives. That layout shift annoys readers and counts towards Cumulative Layout Shift, one of Google's Core Web Vitals. If the CSS already reserves the space, nothing needs doing.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Images with no width and height set
plainWhat: Some images on these pages don't tell the browser their width and height.
The browser may not leave the right space, so text can jump down the page as each image arrives.
That annoys readers and counts against the page in Google's speed measures.
If your site's design already sets the size another way, there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Open one of the pages on a phone and watch whether the text jumps as the images appear.
If it does, ask your developer to add a width and height to the images in the page design.
checks.plainPassed: No image is missing its width and height

checks.title: Broken images
checks.description: The page embeds images () whose URLs return a 4xx or 5xx error or don't respond, directly or after redirects. For images on other sites, statuses often sent only to crawlers (401, 403, 405, 429, 503, 999) don't count.
checks.fix: Point the image's src at a file that loads, or put the file back at the address the page already uses. If the image is gone, choose another or remove the image from the page.
checks.why: Visitors see a broken-image icon or a gap, which makes the page look unfinished, and an image that can't be fetched can't appear in Google Images. A broken image in a template shows up on every page that uses it, so fix those first.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Images that don't load
plainWhat: Some images on these pages don't load: the image file can't be found, or fails with an error.
Visitors see a gap or a broken-image icon, which makes the page look unfinished.
An image in the page design, such as a logo, shows broken on every page that uses it.
plainFix: Open one of the pages in your browser and look for the gap where the image should be.
Upload the image again in your site's editor, or choose another one.
Remove the image from the page if it's no longer needed.
Ask your developer to fix it in the page design if the same image is missing on most pages.
checks.plainPassed: No image fails to load
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly an image in your page design, such as a logo or icon, which every page shares.

checks.title: Large images
checks.description: The page embeds images whose files, after any redirects, are over 200 KB as transferred (the default, which can be changed in the analysis settings).
checks.fix: Replace each file with a smaller one: resize it to the largest size the page shows it at, compress it, and serve it as WebP or AVIF where you can. Where one image is shown at several sizes, offer those sizes with a srcset.
checks.why: Images are often the largest part of a page's weight, and a big one costs visitors time and data, especially on mobile connections. It matters most above the fold, such as a hero image that's the page's Largest Contentful Paint; a large image lazy-loaded far down the page costs much less. The usual causes are photos uploaded straight from a camera and images far larger than the size they're shown at.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Large images that slow pages down
plainWhat: Some pages show images whose files are over 200 KB.
Big images are the most common reason a page feels slow, most of all on a phone, and people leave slow pages.
Photos uploaded straight from a camera or phone are the usual cause.
plainFix: Resize each image so it's no bigger than it's shown on the page.
Save it as a compressed JPEG or WebP, then upload it in place of the old one.
If your site has an image-optimising setting or plugin, turn it on so new uploads are shrunk for you.
checks.plainPassed: No image is too big to load quickly

checks.title: Image without a source
checks.description: The page has elements with no file to show: no src, none of the lazy-loading attributes the crawler reads (data-src and the like), no srcset, not a data: image, and not in a picture element, whose sources show through it. The detail counts them and says which is the first: its alt text, else its class, else where on the page it is. A crawl made before the crawler told data: images apart isn't checked.
checks.fix: Put the image file's address in the image's src attribute. If a lazy-loading script fills the address in, use an attribute lazy-loading scripts commonly use, such as data-src, or the standard loading attribute set to lazy, and check the image still shows without the script.
checks.why: An image with no source doesn't show unless a script gives it one, for visitors or for Google Images. It's usually a template slot left empty, or a lazy-loading script keeping the file in an attribute only it knows, which search engines may not read either. Not an error: a script the crawler doesn't know can look the same.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Images with no picture file named
plainWhat: These pages have image spaces that don't say which picture to show.
Nothing appears there, for visitors or in Google's image search.
It's usually an empty slot in a page design, or code that fills pictures in a way that isn't standard.
plainFix: Open each page and find the empty picture space.
Choose a picture for it in your site's editor, or remove the empty space.
Ask your developer to check how pictures are loaded, if every page has the problem.
checks.plainPassed: Every image names its picture file

checks.title: Large image without srcset
checks.description: The page shows image files at least 800 pixels wide (the default, which can be changed in the analysis settings) with no srcset and not in a <picture> with other sources, so phones download the whole file. It needs the files' pixel sizes, read when the crawl fetched them, so it isn't checked when images weren't fetched. The detail counts them and gives the widest.
checks.fix: On each wide image, offer smaller files with srcset and sizes attributes (for example 480, 800 and 1200 pixels wide), or put the image in a picture element that offers those sources. Most CMSs do this for images uploaded through them.
checks.why: A phone shows a 2,000-pixel image at a few hundred pixels: without other sizes to choose from, it downloads all of it, which costs visitors time and data and slows the page's largest paint. Google Images reads srcset and <picture> too.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Big images sent to phones at full size
plainWhat: These pages show pictures at least 800 pixels wide, with no smaller versions for small screens.
