Phones then download the whole picture, which makes the page slower and uses visitors' data.
plainFix: Upload these pictures through your site's media library, which usually makes smaller versions for phones.
Ask your developer to offer smaller versions of each picture, if your site doesn't.
checks.plainPassed: Big images come in smaller versions for phones

checks.title: Image in an older format
checks.description: The page shows JPEG, PNG, GIF or BMP files of 50 KB or more (the default, which can be changed in the analysis settings), as transferred, and not inside a picture element that offers another source. WebP or AVIF would usually make them smaller. It isn't checked when images weren't fetched. The detail counts them and gives the largest.
checks.fix: Serve each of these files as WebP or AVIF, either as the image's own address or from a picture element that offers a WebP or AVIF source and can keep the older file as a fallback. Most CMSs and image CDNs can convert them.
checks.why: WebP and AVIF usually make photos a quarter to a half smaller at the same quality, and every browser in use shows them, as Google Images does. Smaller images load sooner, above all on phones. 50 KB is about where the newer formats save a noticeable amount.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Images that could be smaller in a newer format
plainWhat: These pages show pictures of 50 KB or more saved in an older format, such as JPEG or PNG.
Newer formats (WebP or AVIF) usually make the same picture a quarter to a half smaller, so pages load faster.
plainFix: Look for an image optimisation setting or plugin that converts pictures to WebP.
Or save the pictures as WebP before you upload them.
checks.plainPassed: No large image is in an older format

checks.title: Alt text that's a file name or too short
checks.description: The page has images whose alt text describes nothing: one or two characters (in an alphabet; in Chinese or Japanese that can be a word), no letter or digit at all, an image file name such as photo.jpg, a camera's or upload's name such as IMG_1234 or image-3, or the image file's own name. An empty alt is right for a decorative image and isn't counted. The detail counts them.
checks.fix: Replace the alt text with a few words that say what the image shows or does, as you would describe it to someone who can't see it. Leave the alt attribute empty for an image that is only decoration.
checks.why: Screen readers read the alt text aloud, and a file name or a stray character tells their users nothing. Google Images uses alt text to understand an image, so a file name is a chance missed.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Image descriptions that don't describe anything
plainWhat: These pages have pictures whose descriptions are a file name, a camera's number such as "IMG_1234", or a stray letter.
People using screen readers hear that instead of what the picture shows, and Google learns nothing from it.
plainFix: Edit each picture in your site's media library and describe what it shows in a few words.
Leave the description empty for a picture that's only decoration.
checks.plainPassed: Every image description says something

checks.title: Image loaded from another website
checks.description: The page shows images straight from another website: not the site's own host or domain, nor an image CDN sites serve their own images from (Shopify's, CloudFront, Cloudinary, imgix, WordPress's i0.wp.com and others). On a crawl started at a private address, other private addresses aren't counted. The detail counts the images and the sites.
checks.fix: Copy the images you have the right to use onto your own site, or a CDN of yours, and show them from there.
checks.why: An image shown from someone else's server can vanish or change whenever they move or block it, and it uses their bandwidth, which many sites refuse. Google Images credits the image to the site it's on, not to yours.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Images shown straight from other websites
plainWhat: These pages show pictures that are stored on other websites, not on yours.
They can disappear or change whenever the other site moves them, and use that site's resources.
plainFix: Check you're allowed to use each picture.
Download the ones you may use and upload them to your own site, then show them from there.
checks.plainPassed: Every image is shown from your own site

checks.title: Large inline (data:) image
checks.description: The page builds images into its HTML as data: URIs larger than 10 KB once decoded (the default, which can be changed in the analysis settings). A crawl made before the crawler measured them isn't checked. The detail counts them and gives the largest, and which it is: its alt text, else its class, else where on the page it is.
checks.fix: Save each inline image as a file and point the image's src attribute at that file, so browsers can cache it and download it separately from the page.
checks.why: An inline image comes with the page every time, can't be cached on its own, and in base64 is a third bigger than the file. A small icon is fine; a photo makes every view of the page slower.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pictures built into the page that slow it down
plainWhat: These pages have pictures of more than 10 KB written into the page itself, not kept as separate files.
They come with the page on every visit and can't be saved by the browser, so every view is slower.
plainFix: Ask your developer to save these pictures as ordinary image files and link to them instead.
checks.plainPassed: No large picture is built into a page

checks.title: Invalid hreflang code
checks.description: An hreflang value on this indexable page isn't a valid code. Valid codes are an ISO 639-1 language, optionally followed by a four-letter script and an ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 region (en, en-GB, zh-Hant-TW), or x-default. UN M.49 numeric regions such as es-419 aren't supported.
checks.fix: Correct the hreflang value to a real language code, with the region after a hyphen when you need one, such as en-GB rather than en-UK, on every page in the set.
checks.why: Google supports only ISO 639-1 languages and ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 regions, and says other codes, such as es-419, aren't supported, so the entry is ignored. An unknown language makes it useless. A reserved region such as UK, EU or UN is different: Google ignores the region and the code still works as the language alone, so en-UK only works as plain en and doesn't target the United Kingdom (whose code is GB). A country code on its own isn't valid either: hreflang="be" means Belarusian, not Belgium.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Language versions labelled with an invalid code
plainWhat: These pages list their versions in other languages, but label one with an invalid language or country code.
Google ignores that entry (an "hreflang" link), or reads only its language, so searchers may be shown the wrong version.
A common slip is "en-UK": the code for the United Kingdom is "GB".
plainFix: Look at the codes the list shows for each page.
Send the list to your developer and ask for each code in the form language, then country, such as "en-GB" or "de-AT".
Ask them to correct it on every page that lists the same versions, not only the ones shown here.
checks.plainPassed: No language version is labelled with an invalid code
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly the list of language versions in your page design, which every page shares.

checks.title: Hreflang without a self-reference
checks.description: This indexable page lists hreflang alternates, but none of them is the page's own URL exactly as crawled.
checks.fix: In this page's head, beside its other hreflang entries, add one whose address is this page's own URL, written exactly as the page is served: scheme, host, path, trailing slash and any query string.
checks.why: Google's rule is that each language version must list itself as well as all the other versions, with the same set of links on every page. Without the self-reference the set breaks that rule and may not be used as intended. Often the self-reference is there but in a different form of the URL, such as http instead of https, without the trailing slash or with a tracking parameter.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Language versions that don't list themselves
plainWhat: These pages list their versions in other languages, but leave their own address out of the list.
Google expects every version to name itself as well as the others, and may ignore a list that doesn't.
Often the page is in its list, but written slightly differently, such as "http" for "https" or without the final slash.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer: this is a change to the code of your pages.
Ask them to add each page's own address to its list of language versions (its "hreflang" links).
Ask them to write it exactly as the page is addressed, with the same "https", "www" and final slash.
checks.plainPassed: No language version leaves itself out of its list

checks.title: Hreflang without return links
checks.description: This indexable page names alternates on the site that are indexable but don't list it in their own hreflang annotations. The detail says how many.
checks.fix: In the head of each alternate, add an hreflang entry that names this page with exactly this URL, and give every page in the set that same complete list.
checks.why: Google requires hreflang to be confirmed from both sides: if page X lists page Y, Y must list X. Where it isn't, Google says the annotations may be ignored or not interpreted correctly, so searchers may be shown the wrong language version. It usually means the sets differ between pages, for example after a new version was added to some templates but not others.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Language versions that don't link back
plainWhat: These pages name versions in other languages that don't name them back.
Google needs both pages to agree before it trusts the pairing, so searchers may be shown the wrong language.
It usually means a new language was added to some pages' lists but not to others.
plainFix: Open one of the pages and a version it names, to confirm that both exist.
Send the list to your developer and ask them to give every version the same full list (of "hreflang" links).
Ask them to make sure each list includes the page itself, at its exact address.
checks.plainPassed: No language version is missing its link back
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one entry in the list of language versions in your page design, which every page shares.

checks.title: Hreflang points to a broken URL
checks.description: This indexable page has hreflang entries whose URLs return a 4xx or 5xx error or don't respond.
checks.fix: Point the entry at the working page for that language, or remove it from every page in the set if that version no longer exists.
checks.why: An alternate that doesn't load can't be shown to anyone and can't confirm the return link, so the entry for that language does nothing, and anyone sent there gets an error. Usually it's a version that was removed or moved without the annotations being updated.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Language versions that lead to a broken page
plainWhat: These pages list a version in another language at an address that doesn't work.
Searchers sent to that version get an error, and the entry for that language does nothing.
Usually the version was removed or moved, and the lists (of "hreflang" links) were never updated.
plainFix: Open the broken address the list shows in your browser, to see the error.
If that version has moved, ask your developer to point the entry at its new address.
If it's gone, ask them to remove the entry from every page that lists it.
checks.plainPassed: No language version leads to a broken page
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one entry in the list of language versions in your page design, which every page shares.

checks.title: Hreflang points to a non-indexable URL
checks.description: This indexable page has hreflang entries whose URLs redirect, are noindex, name another URL as canonical, or are blocked by your robots.txt. Alternates that refused the crawler (a firewall, a bot challenge or a rate limit), and ones on other sites whose robots.txt kept the crawler out, aren't judged: neither says whether search engines can index them. Nor is an x-default entry whose URL redirects temporarily: a home page that sends each visitor on to their language is what x-default is for.
checks.fix: Replace each entry with the alternate's final, canonical, indexable URL, and keep the list identical on every page in the set.
checks.why: Google generally shows each version's canonical, indexable URL in results, so hreflang should name exactly those URLs. An alternate that redirects or is canonicalised elsewhere isn't the URL that gets indexed, and one that's noindex or blocked can't be shown at all, so the entry for that language is unreliable. Google specifically warns against listing HTTP URLs in hreflang when the pages are on HTTPS.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Language versions that search engines can't show
plainWhat: These pages list a version in another language at an address that can't itself appear in search results.
That address forwards elsewhere, is kept out of search, names another page as its main version, or is blocked by your rules file ("robots.txt").
Search engines can't show it, so the entry for that language (an "hreflang" link) can't be relied on.
plainFix: Open the address the list shows in your browser, and see whether it moves you on to a different address.
If it does, ask your developer to list that final address instead.
If it doesn't, ask them to list a version that can appear in search, or to let that one appear.
checks.plainPassed: No language version leads to a page search can't show
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one entry in the list of language versions in your page design, which every page shares.

checks.title: Conflicting hreflang entries
checks.description: This indexable page has the same hreflang code (compared ignoring case) pointing to two or more different URLs. The detail lists the codes.
checks.fix: Keep one URL per code. If two pages really target the same audience, choose one, or give them different regions.
checks.why: Each language or language-region code should name exactly one URL; when a code names several, search engines can't tell which to show for that audience. It's usually two systems adding hreflang, such as a plugin and the theme, or the HTML and an HTTP header, or a copy-paste mistake in the set.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Two addresses listed for the same language
plainWhat: These pages list two or more different addresses for the same language or country.
Search engines can't tell which one to show searchers in that language.
It usually means two parts of your site each add a list (of "hreflang" links), such as a plugin and the page design.
plainFix: Look at the codes the list shows: each is a language that has more than one address.
Check whether your site has two translation or SEO plugins that each add language versions, and turn one off.
Ask your developer to keep one address for each language, if the lists are written in the page design.
checks.plainPassed: No language is listed at two different addresses
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly the list of language versions in your page design, which every page shares.
checks.plainLooksFor: Languages listed at more than one address

checks.title: Hreflang without x-default
checks.description: This indexable page has hreflang annotations but no x-default entry.
checks.fix: In the head of every page in the set, add an alternate link with hreflang set to x-default, pointing at your language selector or the default version.
checks.why: x-default names the page for searchers whose language or region isn't in your list, usually a language selector or the main international version. Google suggests adding one, especially on language or country selectors and home pages that redirect by locale, but it's optional.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Language versions with no fallback page
plainWhat: These pages list their versions in other languages, but name no fallback for everyone else.
The fallback (called "x-default") is the page search engines show when a searcher's language isn't in the list.
Google suggests one but doesn't require it, so if your versions cover your visitors there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Pick the page for visitors whose language you don't cover: usually your language chooser or your main version.
Ask your developer to add it to every page's list of language versions, labelled "x-default".
checks.plainPassed: No list of language versions is missing a fallback page

checks.title: Hreflang outside <head>
checks.description: Some of this indexable page's hreflang links are in the <body> as browsers parse it.
checks.fix: Move the hreflang links into the <head> above anything that could close it early, or declare them in HTTP Link headers or the XML sitemap instead.
checks.why:
Google requires hreflang elements to be inside a well-formed , so these entries don't count and the set is incomplete, which can also break return links from the other versions. Usually the tags are in the head in the source, but an element that doesn't belong there, such as an , a
or stray text, ends the head early.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Language versions written in the wrong part of the page
plainWhat: These pages list some or all of their language versions in a part of the page where search engines ignore them.
The entries there (they're "hreflang" links) don't count, so searchers may be shown the wrong language.
It usually means something added near the top of the page's code, by a plugin or script, has pushed them out of place.
plainFix: Note any plugin, tracking code or banner added to the site lately, as one of them may be the cause.
Send the list to your developer: the hreflang links must sit in the page's "head" section.
Ask them to move or remove whatever ends that section early.
checks.plainPassed: No language version is written in the wrong part of the page

checks.title: Hreflang return link uses another code
checks.description: This indexable page names an alternate under one language code, and the alternate links back but calls itself by another (the page says fr, the alternate fr-ca). A missing return link is another check's. The detail names the first.
checks.fix: Make every page in the set use the same code for each version: the one the version uses for itself.
checks.why: Google asks every version to list itself and all the others; versions that disagree about which language each one is may be ignored, and the wrong version shown to searchers.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Language versions that disagree about their language
plainWhat: These pages point to another language version of themselves, but name its language differently from it.
Google may then ignore the language settings and show the wrong version.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer: it gives the two names each pair uses.
Ask for every version to use the same language name for each page, the one the page uses for itself.
checks.plainPassed: Every language version agrees on its language

checks.title: Hreflang in the HTML and the HTTP header disagree
checks.description: This page gives its language versions both in its HTML and in a Link HTTP header, and the two name different sets. The detail counts each and names what only one has.
checks.fix: Give the versions in one place, or keep both identical: usually the HTML, from your SEO plugin, with the header removed from the server.
checks.why: Google reads both as the same declaration, so sets that differ leave it to guess which is right.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Language versions listed two different ways
plainWhat: These pages list their other language versions twice, in the page and in its server settings, and the two lists differ.
Google can't tell which list is right.
plainFix: Ask your developer to list the language versions in one place only, or to make both lists the same.
checks.plainPassed: Language versions are listed one consistent way

checks.title: Hreflang URL that no page links to
checks.description: An indexable page another page names as a language version, but that no crawled page links to with an ordinary link and no sitemap lists. It's only checked when the crawl read every page that could link to it, and every version hreflang names: the crawl doesn't follow hreflang unless told to, so a version only hreflang leads to is left unread. Where it's found lists the pages naming it.
checks.fix: Link to each language version from the others, such as with a language switcher, and list them in the sitemap.
checks.why: Hreflang says which version to show, not that a page matters: a version only hreflang leads to gets no link signals, and visitors can't reach it from the site.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Language versions that nothing links to
plainWhat: These pages are another page's version in another language, but no page on your site links to them.
Visitors can't reach them, and search engines see them as less important.
plainFix: Add a language switcher, or links between each page's language versions.
List these pages in your sitemap too.
checks.plainPassed: Every language version has links to it

checks.title: Hreflang code and lang attribute differ
checks.description: This indexable page's hreflang entry for itself and its <html lang> name different languages, both written correctly (en against fr; en-GB against en-US is the same language). x-default isn't compared. The detail gives both.
checks.fix: Correct whichever is wrong: the lang attribute in the page's template, or the code your SEO plugin gives this version.
checks.why: Google reads neither to decide a page's language, but screen readers use lang, and two that disagree usually mean one was copied from another version unchanged.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that name two different languages
plainWhat: These pages give one language in their settings for search engines and another in their page code.
One of them is usually wrong, copied from another language version unchanged.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer: it gives the two languages each page names.
Ask them to correct whichever one is wrong.
checks.plainPassed: Every page names one language

checks.title: Hreflang that names only the page itself
checks.description: Every hreflang entry this indexable page has names the page itself (x-default included), so it lists no other language version.
checks.fix: If the site has other language versions, list them all on every version. If it has none, the hreflang entries can go.
checks.why: Hreflang only helps when it links versions of a page in other languages or regions; on its own it does nothing, and it often means the other versions were left out by mistake.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Language settings that list no other language
plainWhat: These pages have language settings for search engines that list only the page itself.
They do nothing on their own: they only help when they point to versions in other languages.
plainFix: If your site has other language versions, list them all on every version.
If it has none, ask your developer to remove the language settings.
checks.plainPassed: Every page's language settings list its other versions

checks.title: Invalid JSON-LD
checks.description: A JSON-LD block (<script type="application/ld+json">) on the page isn't valid JSON. The detail shows the parser's first error: which block, counted in page order, the line and character in the block where it stopped, counted from 1, and why.
checks.fix: In the JSON-LD block, fix the syntax where the detail points: often a comma after the last property, a missing comma, an unescaped quote, or a comment a template left in. Then test the page with Google's Rich Results Test.
checks.why: JSON-LD has to be valid JSON: a trailing comma or a comment is enough for Google to drop the whole block, and its Unparsable structured data report lists the error a trailing comma produces. Nothing in the block is used, so it can't produce a rich result. Other valid blocks on the page still work. A single template error usually breaks the same block on every page that uses it.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Details for search engines that can't be read
plainWhat: Some pages carry details for search engines, such as a product's price, in code that has a mistake in it.
Google ignores the broken details (they're called "structured data"), so the page may lose extras such as star ratings in its results.
One mistake in the page design usually breaks it on every page of that kind.
plainFix: Test one of the pages in Google's Rich Results Test, a free tool on the web, to see the error.
Send the list to your developer: it shows the first error in each page's code (a "JSON-LD" block).
Ask them to fix the page design that writes it, then test the page again.
checks.plainPassed: No details for search engines have a mistake in them
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one mistake in your page design, which writes the same code on every page.

checks.title: Structured data missing required properties
checks.description: A top-level schema.org item on this indexable page, in JSON-LD or Microdata, lacks a property Google requires for that type's rich result. A subtype is held to its parent type's requirements, as a Restaurant is to a LocalBusiness's and a MusicEvent to an Event's. The detail names the type and the missing properties.
checks.fix: Add the missing properties with values that match what's visible on the page, then test it with the Rich Results Test.
checks.why: Google says items missing required properties aren't eligible for rich results, so the markup does nothing for that feature. Recommended properties don't affect eligibility, so they're another check's (Structured data missing recommended properties). FAQPage isn't checked: Google stopped showing FAQ rich results in May 2026. Even complete markup only makes a rich result possible: Google decides whether to show one.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Details for search engines with parts missing
plainWhat: Some pages describe a product, event or similar for search engines, but leave out a detail Google requires.
Without it, Google won't add the extras to your search result, such as stars, prices or dates (a "rich result").
Even complete details only make the extras possible: Google decides whether to show them.
plainFix: Look at what the list says is missing on each page, such as "Product: needs name".
Fill in that detail in your site's editor or shop settings if it's something you enter, such as a price or a date.
If it isn't, ask your developer to add it to the page's "structured data", then test the page in Google's Rich Results Test.
checks.plainPassed: No details for search engines are missing a needed part
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly your page design, which leaves the same detail out of every page of one kind.

checks.title: Structured data that isn't valid schema.org
checks.description: A JSON-LD block or Microdata item on the page has no @context or one that isn't schema.org, a @type schema.org doesn't have, a property schema.org doesn't define for that type or the types it descends from, a date property whose value isn't an ISO 8601 date, or a priceCurrency that isn't an ISO 4217 code. Types and properties written in another vocabulary aren't judged. The detail gives the first three faults.
checks.fix: Correct each fault the detail names, in the JSON-LD block. Spell the type or property as schema.org does (Organization, not Organisation). Write dates as 2026-11-17, or with a time and offset. Write currencies as three-letter codes such as GBP. Put @context at the top of a block that lacks it, set to https://schema.org. Then test the page with the Schema Markup Validator.
checks.why: Search engines read structured data by schema.org's vocabulary: a type or property they don't know, or a date or currency they can't read, is ignored without a word, so the markup may do nothing for the page. Google's Rich Results Test only reports what its own features use, so these faults often go unnoticed.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Product or business details Google can't use
plainWhat: These pages describe a product, article or business for search engines in words that code doesn't have.
Search engines quietly ignore what they can't read, so those details may do nothing for the page.
A misspelt name such as "Organisation", or a date or currency written the wrong way, is the usual cause.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer: it gives the first few mistakes on each page.
If a plugin writes these details, check its settings for dates and currencies, or update it.
checks.plainPassed: All product and business details use words Google knows

checks.title: Structured data missing recommended properties
checks.description: A top-level item on this indexable page lacks properties Google recommends for its type: an Article, NewsArticle or BlogPosting its headline, image, datePublished or author; an Organization its url or logo; a Product its image, or its Offer a priceCurrency or availability. The detail names the type and what it lacks.
checks.fix: Add the properties the detail names, with values that match what's visible on the page. Most SEO and shop plugins have a setting for each, such as the article's featured image or the product's stock status.
checks.why: The markup works without them, but Google uses them for richer results: an article's image and date, a product's price and stock in merchant listings, an organization's logo in knowledge panels. A product needs an image to appear in merchant listings at all.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Product or article details that could be fuller
plainWhat: These pages describe a product, an article or your business for search engines, but leave out details Google asks for.
Nothing is broken, but Google uses them to show more in search, such as an article's picture or a product's price and stock.
A product needs a picture to be shown in Google's shopping results at all.
plainFix: Check the list: it says what each page leaves out.
Fill in the missing details in your site's SEO or shop settings, such as an article's featured image or a product's stock.
Ask your developer to add them, if your site has no such settings.
checks.plainPassed: Every product and article gives the details Google asks for

checks.title: Structured data on a noindex page
checks.description: The page tells search engines not to index it (noindex, in a meta tag or the X-Robots-Tag header) yet has structured data of a type with rich results, such as a Product, Article, Organization or BreadcrumbList, in JSON-LD or Microdata. The detail names the types.
checks.fix: If the page should be in search results, remove the noindex. If it shouldn't, the structured data does nothing there and can stay or go; make sure the indexable page it describes has it instead.
checks.why: Google can't show a rich result for a page it doesn't index, so the markup can't do anything there. It's harmless, and normal where a plugin adds an Organization or BreadcrumbList to every page, but on a product or article it can mean the noindex is a mistake on a page meant to rank.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Product or article details on pages hidden from Google
plainWhat: These pages describe a product or an article for search engines, but also ask not to be shown in search.
Google can't show those details for a page it leaves out, so they do nothing here.
It's harmless, but often a sign that a page meant to be found is hidden by mistake.
plainFix: Check whether each page should appear in search results.
If it should, switch off "hide from search engines" for it in your site's settings.
If it shouldn't, there's nothing to do.
checks.plainPassed: No hidden page carries product or article details

checks.title: Site not on HTTPS
checks.description: The home page (the start URL after its redirects) is served over plain HTTP. Reported once, on the home page.
checks.fix: Install a TLS certificate (free from Let's Encrypt or most hosts), serve every page over HTTPS and 301-redirect each HTTP URL to its HTTPS equivalent. Then update internal links, canonicals and sitemaps, and add HSTS.
checks.why: Browsers label HTTP pages "Not secure", and anything visitors send, such as form data, can be read or changed on the way. Google has used HTTPS as a lightweight ranking signal since 2014 and prefers HTTPS URLs as canonical when both versions exist. Fix this first.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Your site isn't secure (no HTTPS)
plainWhat: Your site doesn't use HTTPS, the secure connection, so nothing sent to or from it is protected.
Browsers label every page "Not secure", and anything a visitor types, such as a password, can be read on the way.
Google prefers the secure version of a page when it has the choice.
This is one fault for the whole site, and the first thing to fix.
plainFix: Open your site with "https://" in front of its address, to see whether a secure version already exists.
Ask your hosting company to switch on HTTPS: most include a free certificate.
Ask them, or your developer, to forward every "http" address to its "https" version (a "301 redirect").
Check the site again, and update any links and settings that still say "http".
checks.plainPassed: The site loads over HTTPS
checks.plainLooksFor: A site that isn't secure (no HTTPS)

checks.title: HTTP page on an HTTPS site
checks.description: This internal page answers over plain HTTP with a page of its own, while the site's home page is on HTTPS.
checks.fix: 301-redirect the HTTP URL to its HTTPS version, ideally for the whole http:// origin at once, and update the links that point at http://.
checks.why: Visitors who reach it get an unencrypted page that browsers label "Not secure", and if an HTTPS version also exists, the two are duplicates for Google to sort out. Usually internal links or a sitemap still point at the http:// URL and the server doesn't redirect it.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages still on the insecure address
plainWhat: These pages still load over "http", without the secure connection the rest of your site uses.
Browsers label them "Not secure", and if an "https" copy exists too, search engines see two copies of the page.
Usually an old link or sitemap entry still points at the "http" address, and nothing forwards it on.
plainFix: Open one of the addresses in your browser and look for "Not secure" beside it.
Ask your developer or hosting company to forward every "http" address to its "https" version (a "301 redirect").
Change the links and sitemap entries that still use "http", so they point at the "https" address.
checks.plainPassed: No page is left on the insecure address

checks.title: Mixed content
checks.description: This HTTPS page loads images, scripts, stylesheets, iframes, audio or video from http:// URLs.
checks.fix: On this HTTPS page, change each resource address from http to https, or to a path on this site, and host a copy of anything whose server has no HTTPS. A Content-Security-Policy that includes upgrade-insecure-requests is a useful safety net.
checks.why: Browsers block insecure scripts, stylesheets and frames on HTTPS pages, which can break layout and features, and upgrade images, audio and video to HTTPS, which then fail to load if the server doesn't offer them that way. Google also lists insecure dependencies other than images among the things that can stop it preferring a page's HTTPS version.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Secure pages that load insecure files
plainWhat: These secure pages load some of their files, such as images or scripts, over an insecure "http" address.
Browsers block some of these files (they call it "mixed content"), so parts of the page can break or go missing.
It's usually an old "http" address left in the page or its design.
plainFix: Open one of the pages in your browser and look for missing images, or a warning beside the address.
Change each address the list shows from "http" to "https", in your site's editor.
If the file is in your page design, ask your developer to change it there.
If the other site has no "https" version, copy the file to your own site or replace it.
checks.plainPassed: No secure page loads an insecure file
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly a file your page design loads on every page, such as a script, style file or logo.

checks.title: Security headers missing
checks.description: The home page's response lacks one or more of Strict-Transport-Security (checked on HTTPS only), X-Content-Type-Options, Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options (or a CSP frame-ancestors rule) and Referrer-Policy. A Content-Security-Policy or a referrer policy the page sets in a meta tag counts as the header would. The detail lists which.
checks.fix: Add the missing headers on the server, CDN or framework, on every page's response. Start with X-Content-Type-Options set to nosniff and a Referrer-Policy, which rarely break anything. Roll out Content-Security-Policy in report-only mode first, and send Strict-Transport-Security only once HTTPS works everywhere on the site.
checks.why: These headers protect visitors: HSTS keeps browsers on HTTPS, CSP limits what injected scripts can do, X-Frame-Options or frame-ancestors stops clickjacking, X-Content-Type-Options stops MIME sniffing, and Referrer-Policy limits which URLs leak to other sites (browsers already default to a safe policy, so it matters least). Google doesn't document them as a ranking factor. Only the home page is checked, as they're normally set site-wide.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Recommended security settings are missing
plainWhat: Your site doesn't send some of the settings that tell browsers how to protect visitors (its "security headers").
They guard against attacks such as someone showing your site inside a fake one.
Only your home page is checked, as these are set once for the whole site.
Search isn't affected and many sites run without them, so this can wait until your developer next works on the site.
plainFix: Send this to your developer or hosting company: the list names the missing settings.
Ask them to add the simple ones first (X-Content-Type-Options and Referrer-Policy), and to test the others before switching them on.
checks.plainPassed: No recommended security setting is missing

checks.title: Security headers set too weakly
checks.description: The home page sends security headers set too weakly: Strict-Transport-Security (on HTTPS) whose max-age is missing, unreadable or under a year (31,536,000 seconds), or X-Content-Type-Options set to anything but nosniff. Checked once, for the whole site, as missing security headers are. The detail names each.
checks.fix: On the server or CDN, send Strict-Transport-Security with a max-age of a year (31536000 seconds) or more, once the whole site works over HTTPS, and set X-Content-Type-Options to nosniff exactly, not a near spelling.
checks.why: HSTS keeps browsers on HTTPS between visits only for as long as its max-age, and the preload list browsers ship asks for a year; a short one lapses between visits. X-Content-Type-Options has one value, nosniff: anything else does nothing.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Security settings that are on but too weak
plainWhat: Your site sends some security settings to browsers, but sets them too weakly to do their job.
One that keeps visitors on the secure version of your site may lapse between visits, for example.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer or hosting company: it says which settings are too weak.
Ask them to strengthen each one, as the list describes.
checks.plainPassed: Your site's security settings are strong enough

checks.title: Cookies without Secure or HttpOnly
checks.description: The page's response sets cookies without basic protection: on HTTPS, without Secure; with SameSite=None but no Secure, which browsers refuse; or a session or login cookie (its name has sess, sid, auth, token, login or jwt) without HttpOnly. Only cookies the server sets are seen, not those a script sets. The detail names each cookie and what it lacks.
checks.fix: In the server's or framework's cookie settings, add the Secure attribute to every cookie on an HTTPS site, and HttpOnly to session and login cookies.
checks.why: A cookie without Secure can be sent over plain HTTP, where it can be read in transit; one without HttpOnly can be read by a script injected into the page, which is how sessions are stolen. Browsers drop a SameSite=None cookie without Secure altogether.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Cookies your site sets without basic protection
plainWhat: These pages store small files in visitors' browsers (cookies) without the basic protections browsers offer.
A login cookie without them could be read by someone else, which is how accounts get taken over.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer: it names each cookie and what it lacks.
Ask them to turn on the cookie protections in your site's settings or code.
checks.plainPassed: Your site's cookies are protected

checks.title: Form sends data over HTTP
checks.description: On an HTTPS page, a form sends what's typed to an http:// address; or on an HTTP page, a form asks for a password. The detail says where it sends. A crawl made before the crawler read forms isn't checked.
checks.fix: Point the form's action at an https address, or a relative address on this site, and serve every page that contains a form over HTTPS.
checks.why: What people type travels unencrypted, where others on the network can read or change it, and browsers warn them before sending it, or mark the page not secure.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Forms that send what people type without encryption
plainWhat: These pages have forms that send what people type over an unencrypted connection.
Others on the same network could read it, and browsers warn visitors before they send it.
plainFix: Ask your developer to make each form send to a secure address, one that starts with https.
If a form plugin made the form, check its settings for the address it sends to.
checks.plainPassed: Every form sends securely

checks.title: Protocol-relative (//) URLs
checks.description: The page has href or src values written without their scheme, starting // (such as //cdn.example.com/app.js), which take the page's own: on an HTTP copy of the page they load over HTTP. An HTTPS page isn't flagged where the home page's Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) header covers its host, as browsers that have been to the site never load an HTTP copy there. Each one a link or a file the page loads is listed with it; the detail counts them all, and names any in a tag that isn't a link or file, such as a resource hint. A crawl made before the crawler noted them isn't checked.
checks.fix: Write each address with https at the front instead of a scheme left off (a leading double slash). The detail names the addresses.
checks.why: They were a way to load the same file over HTTP and HTTPS. On an HTTPS page they load securely anyway, so the risk is an HTTP copy of the page, which HSTS rules out for browsers that have visited. Without HSTS they're worth replacing, and they're an old habit some tools misread.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Links written in an old shortcut style
plainWhat: These pages load files or link to addresses written without their start ("//" instead of "https://").
That shortcut was once common, and still works on a secure page, but it's best replaced.
plainFix: Ask your developer to write each address in full, starting with "https://".
checks.plainPassed: Every address is written in full

checks.title: Uppercase characters in URL
checks.description: This indexable page's URL path contains uppercase letters (percent-escapes such as %2F don't count).
checks.fix: Use lowercase for new URLs. Change an existing one only if it causes duplicates or broken links, with a 301 redirect to the lowercase version and updated internal links.
checks.why: Google treats URLs as case-sensitive, so /Page and /page are different URLs: if the server serves both, mixed-case links create duplicates, and if it doesn't, links typed in lowercase break. Lowercase URLs avoid both. An established URL that works and is linked consistently is fine to leave, since changing it needs redirects.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Addresses with capital letters
plainWhat: These pages have capital letters in their address, such as /About-Us.
Capitals count in an address: /Page and /page are two different addresses, so a link typed in small letters can miss.
An address that works and is always linked the same way is fine to leave, and then there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Use small letters only in the address of every new page.
Leave an existing address alone unless it causes broken links or copies of the page.
If it does, ask your developer to forward it to the small-letter version (a "301 redirect"), and update your links.
checks.plainPassed: No page address has capital letters

checks.title: Underscores in URL
checks.description: This indexable page's URL path contains underscores.
checks.fix: Use hyphens between words in new URLs. Rename existing ones only as part of a wider URL change, with 301 redirects.
checks.why: Google recommends hyphens to separate words in URLs, because underscores are commonly read as joining words (as in format_date) rather than separating them, and hyphens help users and search engines identify the words. The effect is small, so don't change established URLs for this alone.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Addresses with underscores
plainWhat: These pages have underscores in their address, such as /garden_chairs.
Google recommends hyphens instead, as in /garden-chairs, because it reads them as gaps between words.
The gain is small, so there's nothing to do for addresses that already exist.
plainFix: Use hyphens between words in the address of every new page.
Leave existing addresses alone, unless you're changing them for another reason.
If you do change one, ask your developer to forward the old address to the new one (a "301 redirect").
checks.plainPassed: No page address has underscores

checks.title: Long URL
checks.description: This indexable page's URL is longer than 115 characters (the default, which can be changed in the analysis settings), counted as people read it: escapes decoded and an internationalised host in its own script.
checks.fix: Use short, descriptive paths for new pages and keep tracking parameters out of internal links. Shorten existing URLs only with 301 redirects.
checks.why: Google doesn't document a length limit that affects search, and results usually show the domain and a breadcrumb made from parts of the URL rather than the whole thing. Long URLs are mainly harder to read, share and type, and they often point to deep folder structures, keyword-stuffed slugs or tracking parameters worth cleaning up.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Very long addresses
plainWhat: These pages have an address of more than 115 characters.
Search isn't affected, but long addresses are harder to read, share and type.
They often come from folders inside folders, or from tracking codes added to links.
An address that works is fine to leave, and then there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Keep the address short and readable when you make a new page.
Remove tracking codes, such as "?utm_source=newsletter", from links between your own pages.
Leave existing addresses alone, or ask your developer to forward the old address if you shorten one (a "301 redirect").
checks.plainPassed: No page address is very long

checks.title: Internal link with tracking parameters
checks.description: Pages on the site link to this URL of the site's with ad or campaign tracking parameters in its query: utm_source and the other utm_ parameters, gclid, fbclid, msclkid, mc_cid or _ga. The detail names them; where it's found lists the pages linking to it.
checks.fix: On the pages that link here, link to the address without its tracking parameters. Those parameters belong on links from emails, ads and other sites, not between your own pages.
checks.why: Each tagged link is another URL for search engines to crawl and fold into the page they belong to, and analytics counts the visitor as arriving from a new campaign, which breaks up their visit.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: Links between your own pages tagged for ad tracking
plainWhat: Some of your pages link to others with tracking codes meant for ads and emails in the address.
Each such link is another address for search engines, and it muddles your visitor statistics.
plainFix: Find the links on the pages the list names, and remove the tracking codes after the "?" from each address.
checks.plainPassed: No link between your own pages is tagged for tracking

checks.title: URL with multiple slashes
checks.description: This indexable page's path has two slashes in a row (//), which makes it a different URL from the one with a single slash. Where it's found lists the pages linking to it.
checks.fix: Link to the single-slash address, and redirect the double-slash one to it. The usual cause is a template joining a path and a folder that both end or start with a slash.
checks.why: Most servers answer both with the same page, so the site has two URLs for it, which search engines must crawl and fold together.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Addresses with a double slash
plainWhat: These pages' addresses have two slashes in a row.
That makes them different addresses from the single-slash ones, so search engines may see two copies.
plainFix: Change the links to these pages to use a single slash.
Ask your developer to forward each double-slash address to the single-slash one.
checks.plainPassed: No address has a double slash

checks.title: URL with a space
checks.description: This indexable page's path has a space in it (written %20). Where it's found lists the pages linking to it.
checks.fix: Rename the page with hyphens in place of spaces, redirect the old address to it, and update the links.
checks.why: A space isn't allowed in a URL as written, so it's escaped as %20, which reads badly and breaks when the address is copied into emails or documents.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Addresses with spaces in them
plainWhat: These pages' addresses have a space in them, which addresses can't hold as typed.
It shows as "%20", reads badly, and breaks when the address is copied into emails.
plainFix: Rename each page with hyphens in place of the spaces, in your site's editor.
Ask your developer to forward the old addresses to the new ones.
checks.plainPassed: No address has a space in it

checks.title: Indexable URL with parameters
checks.description: This indexable page's URL has a query (a ? part), and it isn't the site's search, which is its own check. The detail names the parameters; where it's found lists the pages linking to it.
checks.fix: If the parameters only sort, filter or track, point this page's canonical link at the same address without them. If the parameters make a page worth finding on its own, give that page a plain address instead.
checks.why: Every combination of parameters is another URL for search engines to crawl, and the same content under many of them divides its signals. Often fine, as for a page of a series, so it's for review.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages whose address has a ? part
plainWhat: These pages can appear in search, and their addresses have a "?" part, as sorting and filtering often add.
Each different "?" part is another address for search engines to visit, often for the same content.
plainFix: Check whether each page is worth finding in search on its own.
If not, ask your developer to point its main address at the version without the "?" part.
checks.plainPassed: No page that can appear in search has a ? part

checks.title: URL with non-ASCII characters
checks.description: This indexable page's path or query, decoded, has characters outside ASCII, such as accented or non-Latin letters. Where it's found lists the pages linking to it.
checks.fix: Nothing is broken: search engines read them. Use ASCII letters, hyphens and digits in new addresses if people will type or share them, and don't rename pages that already rank.
checks.why: URLs are sent as ASCII, so other characters travel percent-encoded (café becomes caf%C3%A9), which some tools, emails and people get wrong when copying.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Addresses with accented or non-English letters
plainWhat: These pages' addresses have accented or non-English letters in them.
Search engines read them fine, but they turn into long codes when copied, which some people and tools get wrong.
plainFix: Use plain letters, hyphens and numbers in new page addresses.
Don't rename pages that already do well in search.
checks.plainPassed: Every address uses plain letters

checks.title: URL with a repeating path
checks.description: This URL of the site's has a path that repeats itself: one segment three times or more, or the same run of segments twice in a row (/shop/shop/, /a/b/a/b/). Only a URL that a page of the crawl links to or uses is judged, and where it's found lists those pages; a URL that only a sitemap lists isn't.
checks.fix: On the pages that link here, find the link that builds the repeating path, usually a relative address such as shop/ that should start with a slash, and fix that link. Redirect this address to the right one.
checks.why: A relative link resolved from the wrong place builds ever-longer URLs, which crawlers can follow without end, each answering with the same page.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: Addresses that repeat themselves
plainWhat: These addresses repeat part of themselves, such as "/shop/shop/".
It's usually a link written slightly wrong, which builds ever-longer addresses for search engines to follow.
plainFix: Look at the pages the list names for the link that leads here.
Ask your developer to correct the link and forward the address to the right page.
checks.plainPassed: No address repeats itself

checks.title: Internal search results page
checks.description: This indexable page is the site's own search: its path has a segment "search", or its query asks something (s, q, query, search, keyword or keywords). The detail names the parameters; where it's found lists the pages linking to it.
checks.fix: In the head of the search results page, add a robots meta tag with noindex, or point its canonical link at a real page, and don't link to search results from the rest of the site.
checks.why: Every search is another page of results that rarely helps anyone who lands on it from a search engine, and there's no end to them for a crawler.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Your site's search results pages show up as pages
plainWhat: Search engines can find and show your site's own search results pages.
They rarely help anyone arriving from a search engine, and there's no end of them to visit.
plainFix: Look in your site's SEO settings or plugin for an option to hide search results from search engines.
Avoid linking to search results from your own pages.
checks.plainPassed: Your site's search results stay out of search engines

checks.title: Slow response
checks.description: The crawler took more than 1,000 ms (the default, which can be changed in the analysis settings) to receive this page's HTML, from request to last byte. The detail also gives the time to first byte.
checks.fix: If the first byte is slow, find what the server waits on: add caching, speed up database queries and back-end calls, and serve from a CDN near your visitors. If the download after it is slow, reduce the HTML size.
checks.why: Nothing on the page can render until its HTML arrives, so a slow response delays everything visitors see; web.dev's rough guide is a time to first byte of 0.8 seconds or less. Google also crawls less when a site's response times get longer, which matters mainly for large sites. Times depend on the crawler's location and speed preset, so recheck a few slow pages before acting.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that are slow to answer
plainWhat: These pages took more than 1 second to arrive when the check asked for them.
Nothing can appear on screen until the page arrives, so visitors wait, and Google visits slow sites less often.
One slow reading can be a blip, so try the pages yourself before acting.
plainFix: Open two or three of the pages in your browser and see whether they're slow for you too.
If they are, send the list to your developer or hosting company and ask what the server is waiting for.
Ask about page caching and a faster hosting plan: they're the usual fixes.
checks.plainPassed: No page is slow to answer

checks.title: Large HTML
checks.description: This page's HTML is larger than 1 MB once decompressed (the default, which can be changed in the analysis settings). Images, scripts and stylesheets loaded as separate files don't count.
checks.fix: Move inline scripts, styles, framework data and base64 images into separate cacheable files, paginate very long lists, and keep the main content and links early in the HTML.
checks.why: Large HTML takes longer to download and parse, especially on phones. Googlebot reads only the first 2 MB of an HTML file, measured uncompressed, for Google Search, and ignores the rest; a page past that limit is reported on its own. The bulk is usually inline scripts, framework state data, inline SVG or base64 images.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages with a lot of code to download
plainWhat: These pages have more than 1 MB of code in the page itself, before any images or other files.
A page that heavy takes longer to arrive and to appear, most of all on a phone.
Google also stops reading a page at 2 MB, which is listed as a problem of its own.
Below 2 MB, a page that still feels quick on a phone needs nothing done.
plainFix: Open one of the pages on a phone and see whether it's slow to appear.
If it is, send the list to your developer: it shows each page's size.
Ask them to move scripts, styles and images that are written into the page out into separate files, and to split very long lists.
checks.plainPassed: No page has too much code to download

checks.title: HTML past Google's crawl limit
checks.description: This page's HTML is larger than 2 MB once decompressed, which is as far as Googlebot reads a file for Google Search. Images, scripts and stylesheets loaded as separate files don't count. The limit is Google's, not an analysis setting.
checks.fix: Move inline scripts, styles, framework data and base64 images into separate files, and keep the main content and links within the first 2 MB.
checks.why: Googlebot stops at the first 2 MB of the uncompressed file and ignores everything after it, so content and links past that point aren't indexed or followed for Google Search. Other Google fetchers use different limits. The usual cause is inline scripts, framework data, inline SVG or base64 images pushing the real content past the cut-off.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages too big for Google to read in full
plainWhat: These pages have more than 2 MB of code in the page itself, which is as far as Google reads.
Google ignores everything after that point, so text and links near the end of the page aren't seen.
The bulk is usually scripts, styles or images written into the page instead of loaded as separate files.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer: it shows each page's size.
Ask them to move scripts, styles and images that are written into the page out into separate files.
Ask them to put the main text and links early in the page, within the first 2 MB.
checks.plainPassed: No page is too big for Google to read in full

checks.title: Script or stylesheet over 2 MB
checks.description: A page uses this script or stylesheet, here or on another site, and it's larger than 2 MB, as far as Googlebot reads a file. It's measured once decompressed, which is what Google's limit is of, and the detail gives the size it was sent at beside it when the server compressed it. A crawl made before version 2.1.1 only has the size as sent, so it misses a compressed file that is over the limit once decompressed: crawl again to measure those. The limit is Google's, not an analysis setting.
checks.fix: Split the file, or remove what pages don't use (unused code, inlined data, source maps); load what isn't needed at first later. Compressing the file doesn't help here: Google's limit is on its size once decompressed.
checks.why: Google fetches each script and stylesheet a page uses separately, with the same 2 MB limit as the page, and ignores the rest of a larger one, so the page as Google renders it can be missing styles or behaviour, or break. A file that size also slows the page down for visitors on mobile.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: Code files too big for Google to read in full
plainWhat: These code or style files are bigger than the part of each file Google reads.
Google ignores the rest, so it may see your pages without some of their look or how they work.
Files that big also make pages slow on phones.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer, with the size of each file.
Ask them to split each file, or to remove what your pages don't use.
checks.plainPassed: No code file is too big for Google to read in full

checks.title: Missing viewport
checks.description: The page has no viewport meta tag (<meta name="viewport">) with content.
checks.fix: In the page's head, add a viewport meta tag with width set to device-width and initial-scale set to 1, then check the layout really adapts to small screens.
checks.why: Without it, mobile browsers lay the page out at a desktop width (about 980 pixels) and shrink it to fit, so text is tiny and visitors have to zoom and pan. Google indexes pages as its smartphone crawler sees them, and its page experience guidance asks whether content displays well on mobile devices.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages not set up for phones
plainWhat: These pages lack the line of code that tells a phone to fit the page to its screen.
Phones show them as a tiny copy of the desktop page, so visitors must zoom and scroll sideways to read.
Google reads every page as a phone would, so this is the version it judges.
plainFix: Open one of the pages on a phone and see whether the text is too small to read.
Ask your developer to add the missing line (a "viewport" setting) to the page design.
Ask them to check the page design really adapts to small screens, as the line alone won't do it.
checks.plainPassed: No page is missing its phone-screen setting

checks.title: Missing lang attribute
checks.description: The page's <html> element has no lang attribute, or it's empty.
checks.fix: Set the lang attribute on the html element to the page's main language, such as en-GB, and mark any passage in another language with its own lang.
checks.why: Screen readers use lang to choose the right voice and pronunciation, and WCAG requires the page's language to be set this way; browsers use it too, for example for hyphenation. Google doesn't: it detects the language from the visible content, so this is about accessibility, not search.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that don't say what language they're in
plainWhat: These pages don't state in their code which language they're written in.
Screen readers use that to pick the right voice, so without it they may read the page in the wrong accent.
Google works the language out from the text itself, so search isn't affected and this can wait.
plainFix: Check your site's settings for a "site language" option, and set it if it's empty.
Ask your developer to add the language to the page design (a "lang" setting, such as "en-GB") if there's no such option.
checks.plainPassed: Every page says what language it is in

checks.title: Missing character encoding
checks.description: Nothing declares the page's character encoding where browsers look for it: no byte-order mark at the start of the file, no charset in the Content-Type header, and no meta tag (<meta charset> or http-equiv Content-Type) within the first 1024 bytes. The detail says where a meta tag further in ends.
checks.fix: Declare UTF-8 either as a charset meta tag that is the first element in the head, within the first 1024 bytes of the file, or as charset=utf-8 on the Content-Type response header.
checks.why: Without a declaration, browsers have to guess the encoding, and a wrong guess turns accented letters, currency symbols and curly quotes into garbled characters. W3C advises always declaring it, even when a page happens to display correctly. A page that starts with a byte-order mark has declared it, and isn't reported; a crawl made before the crawler recorded the mark still reports such a page, until it's crawled again. Likewise a crawl made before the crawler recorded where the meta tag ends passes one past the first 1024 bytes.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages at risk of showing garbled characters
plainWhat: These pages don't tell browsers how their letters and symbols were saved, or tell them too far down the page.
Browsers have to guess, and a wrong guess turns accents, £ signs and curly quotes into nonsense.
Pages that look right today can wait, but the one-line fix removes the risk.
plainFix: Open one of the pages and look for odd symbols where accents, £ signs or quote marks should be.
Ask your developer to state the character set in the page design (a "charset" line, set to "utf-8").
checks.plainPassed: No page leaves browsers guessing its characters

checks.title: Open Graph tags missing
checks.description: This indexable page lacks og:title, og:description or og:image, or has them empty. The detail says which are missing and which are empty.
checks.fix: In the page's head, add the og:title, og:description and og:image meta tags. The image must be a full URL of a picture of this page, not the site logo. Most SEO plugins fill these from the title, the meta description and the featured image.
checks.why: Social networks and chat apps build link previews from Open Graph tags; without them they guess the title and image or show a bare link. Google also lists og:title among its sources for title links and accepts og:image as a way to suggest a page's preferred image. Low priority for pages nobody shares.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that won't preview well when shared
plainWhat: These pages lack the title, description or image that apps show when someone shares a link.
Without them (they're called "Open Graph tags"), the preview is a guess, or a bare link.
It matters only for pages people are likely to share: for the rest there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Find the page's "social sharing" or "social preview" settings in your site's editor.
Add a title, a short description and an image.
If there's no such setting, ask your developer to add Open Graph tags to the page design.
checks.plainPassed: Every page has its sharing preview details
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly your page design, which leaves the same details out of every page.

checks.title: X (Twitter) card missing
checks.description: This indexable page has no twitter:card meta tag (by name or property), so X shows its link without a card.
checks.fix: In the page's head, add a twitter:card meta tag, using the name attribute rather than property, with the content summary_large_image. Most SEO plugins do this with one setting. X uses the Open Graph title, description and image when the twitter tags for them are absent.
checks.why: X reads twitter:card to choose a card; without it, a shared link gets no image or a small one. It falls back to Open Graph for everything else, so the one tag is usually all a page needs.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages without a preview card for X
plainWhat: These pages don't say which kind of preview X (Twitter) should show when someone shares them.
X then shows a plain link, or a small preview, instead of a card with a picture.
plainFix: Turn on X (Twitter) cards in your SEO plugin or theme settings.
If there's no setting, ask your developer to add an X card to every page.
checks.plainPassed: Every page has a preview card for X

checks.title: X (Twitter) card incomplete
checks.description: This indexable page asks for an X card that can't be built: its type isn't summary, summary_large_image, app or player; it has no title (twitter:title, else og:title); a summary card has no image (twitter:image, else og:image); a player card has no twitter:player; or its twitter: tags are written only with property=, which X doesn't read. The detail gives each fault. A crawl made before the crawler told name= from property= isn't checked.
checks.fix: In the head, fill in the twitter tag the detail says is missing. Write twitter tags with the name attribute, not property: a tag written with property is ignored.
checks.why: X builds a card only from the tags it reads; with a part missing it shows a bare link, so the card tag does nothing.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Preview cards for X that are missing parts
plainWhat: These pages ask X (Twitter) for a preview card, but leave out something the card needs, such as a title or a picture.
X can't build the card, so people see a plain link instead.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer: it says what each page's card lacks.
Ask them to fill in the missing parts, or to write the card the way X reads it.
checks.plainPassed: Every preview card for X is complete

checks.title: Open Graph or X image URL isn't absolute
checks.description: This indexable page's og:image (og:image:url, og:image:secure_url) or twitter:image isn't a full http:// or https:// URL: a path such as /img/share.jpg, or one starting with //. The detail gives the first.
checks.fix: Set the Open Graph or X image to a full URL, starting with https and your domain, not a path on its own.
checks.why: The Open Graph protocol gives its URLs with http:// or https://, and networks fetch the image on their own: a relative path may be read from the wrong place or not at all, and the share shows no image.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Share images given an incomplete address
plainWhat: These pages name the picture to show when they're shared, but give only part of its address.
Facebook, X and others need the full address, so they may show no picture.
plainFix: Ask your developer to give the full address of each share picture, starting with https://.
checks.plainPassed: Every share picture has its full address

checks.title: og:url isn't the page's address
checks.description: This indexable page's og:url, normalised, is another URL than its own: often every page's points at the home page. An indexable page's canonical is itself, so that's what og:url should give. The detail gives it, grouped by it, so a template's is one group.
checks.fix: Set the og:url meta tag to this page's own URL, or remove the tag so networks use the address that was shared.
checks.why: The Open Graph protocol defines og:url as the canonical URL of the object. Networks gather shares, likes and the preview under it, so one that names another page credits that page and sends clicks there.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Share links that point to a different page
plainWhat: These pages tell social networks that their address is another page's, often your home page.
Shares and likes then count toward that page, and people who click the share land there.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer: it gives the address each page names.
Ask them to make each page name its own address, or leave the setting out.
checks.plainPassed: Every page names its own address for sharing

checks.title: Open Graph or X tag repeated
checks.description: This indexable page gives og:title, og:description, og:url, og:type, twitter:card, twitter:title or twitter:description more than once, with different content. og:image and the other properties that take several values may repeat. The detail counts each and quotes its different values, as 2 og:title: "Sofas" · "Chairs".
checks.fix: Keep one of each Open Graph or X tag in the head. Two plugins, or a plugin and the theme, are usually both writing them: turn one off.
checks.why: Each of these says one thing about the page; given twice with different values, each network picks one its own way, and it may not be the one you meant.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Share settings given twice with different values
plainWhat: These pages give the same share setting, such as the title to show, twice, with different words.
Social networks pick one of them, and it may not be the one you want.
plainFix: Look for two plugins or a plugin and your theme both adding share settings, and turn one of them off.
If that isn't it, ask your developer to remove the copy.
checks.plainPassed: No share setting is given twice

checks.title: Duplicate og:title
checks.description: Indexable pages share an og:title (or the twitter:title where it has none) while their <title>s differ: pages whose <title>s are the same are title-duplicate's, and their og:titles usually follow. A page whose og:title is its own title isn't flagged: it's the one the others copied. Grouped by the shared text.
checks.fix: Give each page its own og:title, usually by letting the SEO plugin fill it from the page's title.
checks.why: Shared on a network, pages with one og:title look the same, however different they are: a template's fixed og:title is the usual cause.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that share the same title when shared
plainWhat: These pages have different titles in search, but show the same title when they're shared on social networks.
People who see the shares can't tell the pages apart.
plainFix: Give each page its own share title in your SEO plugin, or leave it empty so the page's own title is used.
checks.plainPassed: Every page has its own share title

checks.title: Duplicate og:description
checks.description: Indexable pages share an og:description (or the twitter:description where it has none) while their meta descriptions differ. A page whose og:description is its own meta description isn't flagged: it's the one the others copied, as with a platform that gives every page without a description the home page's. Grouped by the shared text.
checks.fix: Give each page its own og:description, usually by letting the SEO plugin fill it from the page's meta description.
checks.why: Shared on a network, pages with one og:description say the same under their titles, whatever they're about.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that share the same summary when shared
plainWhat: These pages have different summaries in search, but show the same summary when they're shared on social networks.
Each share then says the same thing, whatever the page is about.
plainFix: Give each page its own share summary in your SEO plugin, or leave it empty so the page's own description is used.
checks.plainPassed: Every page has its own share summary

checks.title: Open Graph or X image broken
checks.description: This indexable page's og:image or twitter:image is broken (after any redirects), or answers with something other than an image, such as a page. Only checked when the crawl fetched images. The detail gives the first.
checks.fix: Point the tag at an image that loads, or upload the missing image again.
checks.why: A network that can't load the share image shows the link without one. Only link previews suffer, so it's a notice.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Share images that don't load
plainWhat: The picture these pages name for social networks doesn't load: it's missing, or it isn't a picture.
Shares of these pages show no picture.
plainFix: Choose a new share picture for each page in your SEO plugin, or upload the missing one again.
checks.plainPassed: Every share picture loads

checks.title: Open Graph or X image over 5 MB
checks.description: This indexable page's og:image or twitter:image is over 5 MB, as received. Where a page names several, the first of each is judged: it's the one networks show. Only checked when the crawl fetched images.
checks.fix: Use a smaller copy: 1,200 × 630 pixels, saved as JPEG or WebP, is well under 1 MB.
checks.why: X doesn't show an image over 5 MB; Facebook's limit is 8 MB, and a large file is slow to fetch for every preview.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Share images too big to show
plainWhat: The picture these pages name for social networks is larger than 5 MB.
X won't show a picture that large, and other networks are slow to load it.
plainFix: Save a smaller copy of each picture, under 1 MB is plenty, and choose it as the share picture.
checks.plainPassed: No share picture is too big

checks.title: Open Graph or X image too small
checks.description: This indexable page's og:image is under 200 × 200 pixels, or the image X uses (twitter:image, else og:image) is under 300 × 157 on a summary_large_image card or 144 × 144 on a summary card. The proportions aren't judged: both networks crop. Where a page names several images, the first of each tag is judged: it's the one networks show. Only checked when the crawl fetched images.
checks.fix: Use an image at least 1,200 × 630 pixels, which suits every network.
checks.why: Facebook rejects an image under 200 × 200 pixels and recommends 1,200 × 630; X shows a small image blurred, or none.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Share images too small to show well
plainWhat: The picture these pages name for social networks is smaller than they need.
Facebook won't use a picture under 200 pixels square, and X shows a small one blurred or not at all.
plainFix: Choose a larger share picture for each page: 1,200 by 630 pixels suits every network.
checks.plainPassed: Every share picture is large enough

checks.title: Head tags in the body
checks.description: Tags that belong in the are in the as browsers and Google parse the page: the ; a meta description, robots, viewport or the like; Open Graph or X tags; or a <link rel="alternate"> without hreflang. Usually an element that can't be in a head, such as a <div>, an <img> or stray text, ended the head early and pushed every tag after it into the body; the detail names what's out and what ended the head. Canonical and hreflang links have their own checks. A crawl made before the crawler noted these isn't checked.
checks.fix: Move the element that ended the head early into the body, or remove it; tags written in the body by mistake belong in the <head>. A plugin or tag manager that injects an element high in the head is the usual cause.
checks.why: Search engines and social sites may ignore page settings that aren't in the head: Google says so of canonicals, and treats the rest as it can. One stray element moves every tag after it, so a whole template's titles, descriptions and robots rules can be out at once.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Page settings that ended up where they're ignored
plainWhat: Some settings these pages give search engines and social sites, such as the title, are where they may be ignored.
