Usually something placed too early on the page, such as a banner or a tracking code, pushed them out of place.
The list says which settings moved, and what moved them.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer: it names what moved the settings on each page.
Ask them to move that item further down the page, or remove it.
checks.plainPassed: Every page setting is where search engines read it
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one item in your page design or a plugin, which every page shares.

checks.title: HTML document structure errors
checks.description: The page's HTML has a second <head> or <body> start tag, an <html> tag after content, or a <head> after the body has begun, which the HTML standard counts as errors. A missing <head> or <body> tag isn't one: both are optional. The detail says which, and on which line of the page's HTML the tag at fault is. A crawl made before the crawler noted them isn't checked.
checks.fix: Fix the template so the page has one <html>, one <head> and one <body>, in that order, with nothing before the <html>. Content printed before the page starts, such as a server warning, is a common cause.
checks.why: Browsers recover from these the same way every time, merging or dropping the extra tags, so visitors rarely notice. But the attributes on the second tag are lost, and the same fault can move tags out of the head.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages whose basic HTML structure is broken
plainWhat: The code of these pages has some of its basic parts twice, or out of order.
Browsers fix this the same way every time, so visitors rarely notice, but some settings on the second part are lost.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer: it says what's wrong on each page.
Ask them to fix the page design so each page has its parts once, in order.
checks.plainPassed: No page has its basic structure broken

checks.title: Viewport that disables zoom or sets no width
checks.description: The page's viewport meta tag stops visitors zooming (user-scalable=no or 0, or a maximum-scale under 2), sets neither width nor initial-scale, or the page has two viewport tags that differ. The detail lists the faults.
checks.fix: In the head, keep a single viewport meta tag whose content sets width to device-width and initial-scale to 1, and remove maximum-scale, user-scalable set to no, and any other limit on zoom.
checks.why: Stopping zoom fails people who need larger text, which WCAG requires to work up to 200%, and some browsers ignore it anyway. A viewport with no width lays the page out at desktop width on phones, as a missing one does.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages people can't zoom, or that don't fit phones
plainWhat: These pages stop visitors zooming in on phones, or don't tell phones how wide to show them.
People who need larger text can't read them, and a page with no width shows tiny on a phone.
plainFix: Ask your developer to set the phone-screen setting to the standard "width=device-width, initial-scale=1", with nothing that limits zoom.
checks.plainPassed: Every page lets people zoom and fits phones

checks.title: Character encoding declared wrongly
checks.description: The page's character encoding, as a byte-order mark, the Content-Type header or the meta tag declares it, isn't UTF-8; or the header and the meta tag name different encodings (the header wins); or the page has two meta declarations that differ. A meta tag after the first 1024 bytes declares nothing: with the header declaring the encoding it changes nothing, and without it that's a missing encoding. The detail says which.
checks.fix: Save and serve the page as UTF-8: name UTF-8 as the charset in the Content-Type header, and put one meta charset tag naming UTF-8 first in the head.
checks.why: The HTML standard requires UTF-8. A page in another encoding usually shows right, but a declaration that's wrong or contradicts another makes browsers guess, and a wrong guess garbles accented letters, currency symbols and quotes.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that name the wrong text encoding
plainWhat: These pages say they use a text encoding other than the standard one (UTF-8), or say two different things about it.
Browsers then have to guess, and a wrong guess turns accents, currency signs and quotes into garbled characters.
plainFix: Ask your developer to save and serve every page as UTF-8, and to declare it once, at the top of the page.
checks.plainPassed: Every page names its text encoding correctly

checks.title: Invalid lang attribute
checks.description: The page's <html lang> isn't a well-formed language tag: a 2-letter ISO 639-1 language (or a 3-letter one), then optionally a 4-letter script and a 2-letter region or 3-digit area, all separated by hyphens, such as en, en-GB or zh-Hant-TW. en_GB, english and uk-en aren't. The detail gives the value.
checks.fix: Set the html element's lang attribute to the page's language code, such as en or en-GB: a hyphen, not an underscore, and the language before the region.
checks.why: Screen readers use lang to choose the voice and pronunciation, and browsers for hyphenation and spelling; a value they can't read is as good as none. Google detects a page's language from its content, so this is about accessibility, not search.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that name their language wrongly
plainWhat: These pages give their language as something that isn't a language code, such as "english" or "en_GB".
Screen readers then can't tell which voice to use, so the page may be read out in the wrong accent.
plainFix: Change the page's language setting to a code such as "en" or "en-GB": a hyphen, not an underscore, with the language first.
checks.plainPassed: Every page names its language correctly

checks.title: Separate mobile URL
checks.description: The page names a separate mobile version with <link rel="alternate" media="…"> (without hreflang). The detail gives its URL. A crawl made before the crawler noted these isn't checked.
checks.fix: If the site has a separate mobile site, make sure each mobile page has a rel="canonical" back to its desktop page and the same content; consider moving to one responsive page per URL.
checks.why: Google indexes the mobile version of pages, and still supports separate mobile URLs if the alternate and canonical links pair them up, but recommends responsive design: one URL is simpler to keep right, and a mobile site that has less content than the desktop one loses it in search.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages with a separate mobile version
plainWhat: These pages point to a separate version of themselves for phones, at another address.
Google still supports that, but a single page that fits every screen is simpler to keep right.
plainFix: Check that each mobile page names this page as its main version.
If you're redesigning, consider one page that fits every screen instead.
checks.plainPassed: No page has a separate mobile version
